ABSTRACTPost-quantum migration is a critical challenge for enterprise blockchain systems that rely
on classical digital signatures. Hyperledger Fabric extensively uses ECDSA for identity management,
endorsement, TLS, and transaction validation, making a full infrastructure-level migration complex. This
paper presents a controlled empirical evaluation of a hybrid ML-DSA-65/ECDSA signature architecture for
Hyperledger Fabric. The proposed approach preserves Fabric’s native ECDSA-based infrastructure while
integrating ML-DSA-65 at the application layer through an external post-quantum signing microservice.
ML-DSA-65 signatures and public keys are stored on-ledger as application-level cryptographic evidence,
providing an incremental post-quantum signature layer without modifying Fabric core binaries. The scope of
this protection is intentionally limited: Fabric’s native MSP/X.509 identities, peer endorsement signatures,
TLS-protected communications, block-level metadata signatures, and ordering-service communications
remain based on classical cryptography in the evaluated deployment. The implementation is evaluated
on a deployed Fabric network with two organizations, four peers, three Raft orderers, CouchDB state
databases, and Go chaincode deployed as Chaincode-as-a-Service. A latency-matched ECDSA baseline
is compared with the PQC hybrid configuration across six scenarios covering throughput, latency, stress
behavior, payload robustness, resource consumption, cryptographic primitive performance, and block-size
overhead. Results show that optimized ML-DSA-65 signing achieves an average latency of 0.226 ms, while
no statistically significant degradation was detected in the primary transaction-level performance metrics
under the tested workloads. The main measured operational cost is storage-related: active blocks in the ML-
DSA-65 configuration are approximately 1.43×larger than those of the functionally equivalent application-
layer ECDSA P-256 baseline for signing-intensive transactions. These results indicate that application-layer
hybrid ML-DSA-65/ECDSA signatures offer a practical incremental migration path for enterprise Fabric
deployments, with ledger growth rather than transaction processing performance as the principal measured
trade-off.

Caliper; ledger storage overhead.

evident transaction records. Among these platforms, Hy-
perledger Fabric is widely adopted because of its modular
architecture, membership-based identity model, configurable
endorsement policies, and separation between transaction ex-

in blockchain systems. However, migrating blockchain in-

in blockchain systems. However, migrating blockchain in-
frastructures from ECDSA to post-quantum signatures is not
a simple algorithm replacement. Post-quantum signatures
are substantially larger than ECDSA signatures, and their

This challenge is particularly significant in Hyper-
ledger Fabric. Unlike public blockchains where trans-
action signatures are often evaluated primarily at the
transaction-authentication layer, Fabric integrates cryptog-
raphy across multiple components, including Membership
Service Providers (MSPs), X.509 certificates, endorsement
signatures, transaction envelopes, TLS channels, ordering
services, and block validation. A complete post-quantum mi-
gration of Fabric would therefore require changes to several
infrastructure layers. Such deep modifications may introduce
compatibility, maintainability, and deployment challenges,
especially in enterprise environments where blockchain net-
works are operated by multiple organizations and governed
by strict change-management procedures.
Hybrid migration has emerged as a practical strategy
for the transition period. Instead of immediately replacing
all classical cryptographic mechanisms, hybrid approaches
combine classical and post-quantum primitives to preserve
backward compatibility while introducing resistance against
future quantum adversaries [5]–[7]. In the context of Fabric,
an application-layer hybrid approach is attractive because it
allows post-quantum transaction authentication to be intro-
duced without modifying Fabric’s native MSP, BCCSP, TLS,
or endorsement mechanisms. Nevertheless, the practical cost
of such an approach must be evaluated empirically at the
system level.
The proposed architecture occupies a different PQC in-
tegration point from previous post-quantum extensions of
Hyperledger Fabric. PQFabric [8] integrates hybrid post-
quantum mechanisms within Fabric’s cryptographic and
credential-management stack, whereas Abbas et al. [9] ex-
tend the identity-provisioning process to incorporate post-
quantum key material into Fabric credentials. In contrast,
the present work introduces ML-DSA-65 through an external
application-layer ML-DSA signing service while retaining
the native Fabric MSP, BCCSP, TLS, endorsement, and
transaction-validation mechanisms unchanged in the evalu-
ated deployment. The proposed approach therefore investi-
gates a different migration trade-off: reduced integration in-
trusiveness and independent evolution of the PQC component
in exchange for intentionally limited post-quantum coverage.
Accordingly, the proposed architecture should be interpreted
as an incremental application-layer PQC migration strategy
rather than a fully quantum-safe Hyperledger Fabric imple-
mentation.
Existing studies on post-quantum blockchain systems
provide important insights into cryptographic primitives,
blockchain simulations, certificate-level modifications, and
application-specific architectures. However, there remains
a gap in controlled empirical evaluations of hybrid post-
quantum digital signatures in a deployed Hyperledger Fabric
network. In particular, limited evidence is available regard-
ing how application-layer ML-DSA signatures affect Fabric
throughput, latency, stress behavior, payload sensitivity, CPU
and memory consumption, and on-ledger block-size growth
under repeated benchmark runs and statistical analysis.
This paper addresses this gap by designing and evaluating
a hybrid ML-DSA-65/ECDSA signature architecture for Hy-
perledger Fabric. The proposed approach preserves Fabric’s
native ECDSA-based identity, endorsement, and validation
pipeline while adding ML-DSA-65 signatures at the appli-
cation layer through an external post-quantum signing mi-
croservice. The resulting ML-DSA-65 signature and public
key are stored on-ledger as application-level cryptographic
evidence without requiring modifications to Fabric core bi-
naries.

II. RELATED WORK
A. QUANTUM THREAT, PQC STANDARDIZATION, AND
HYBRID MIGRATION
Public-key cryptography constitutes a fundamental security
layer for digital infrastructures, including public-key infras-
tructures, secure communication protocols, and blockchain-
based transaction systems. Classical public-key mechanisms
such as RSA, DSA, and elliptic-curve cryptography rely
on the computational hardness of integer factorization and
discrete logarithm problems. However, Shor’s quantum al-
gorithm demonstrated that these problems can be solved in
polynomial time on a sufficiently powerful quantum com-
puter, thereby threatening the long-term security of widely
deployed public-key schemes, including ECDSA [2]. This
threat is particularly relevant for blockchain systems, where
digital signatures are used to authorize transactions, au-
thenticate participants, and preserve non-repudiation. Since
ECDSA remains a common classical signature baseline in
many blockchain architectures, including permissioned and
permissionless systems, its vulnerability under the quantum
threat model motivates the transition toward post-quantum
alternatives [3].
Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) aims to provide cryp-
tographic primitives resistant to both classical and quantum
adversaries. Several families of PQC have been explored,
including lattice-based, hash-based, code-based, multivari-
ate, and isogeny-based cryptography [10]. Among them,
lattice-based cryptography has emerged as a leading direc-
tion because it offers a favorable balance between secu-
rity assumptions, implementation efficiency, and practical
deployability. Its security foundations rely on hard lattice
problems such as Learning With Errors (LWE), Short Integer
Solution (SIS), and their structured module variants [11],
[12]. CRYSTALS-Dilithium is one of the most prominent
lattice-based digital signature schemes and was selected
during the NIST post-quantum cryptography standardiza-
tion process [13]. Its standardized version, ML-DSA, is
specified in NIST FIPS 204 and provides a module-lattice-
based digital signature standard for post-quantum authenti-
cation [4]. This need for proactive migration is reinforced
by quantum-risk analyses emphasizing that cryptographic
transition must begin before the availability of cryptograph-
ically relevant quantum computers [14]. Recent surveys also
highlight hybrid cryptographic frameworks combining clas-
sical and post-quantum primitives, including ECDSA with
Dilithium for dual-signature authentication [15]. Although
standardization provides an essential foundation for migra-
tion, the transition from classical signatures to post-quantum
signatures is not merely a matter of replacing one algorithm
with another. Existing systems depend on classical public-
key infrastructures, certificate formats, identity management
mechanisms, authentication protocols, and interoperability
constraints. For this reason, several studies have empha-
sized the importance of hybrid migration strategies, where
classical and post-quantum mechanisms coexist during the
transition period [5]–[7]. Such hybrid approaches aim to
preserve compatibility with existing infrastructures while
adding protection against future quantum adversaries. This
is especially important for permissioned blockchain sys-
tems such as Hyperledger Fabric, where X.509 certificates,
membership service providers, endorsement signatures, and
transaction validation mechanisms are deeply integrated into
the system architecture. Earlier surveys also reviewed the
impact of quantum computing on blockchain cryptography
and identified post-quantum signatures as a key migration
direction for blockchain systems [16]. Recent migration-
oriented studies have also highlighted the importance of eval-
uating not only the cryptographic security of post-quantum
primitives, but also their operational impact. Larger public
keys and signatures may affect communication overhead,
certificate size, transaction size, block propagation, storage
growth, and validation cost. In blockchain environments,
these effects are amplified because signatures are not isolated
protocol artifacts; they become part of transaction envelopes,
endorsement payloads, and ledger records. Consequently, the
feasibility of hybrid or fully post-quantum migration must

B. POST -QUANTUM DIGITAL SIGNATURES FOR
BLOCKCHAIN SYSTEMS
Digital signatures are central to blockchain security. They
provide transaction authenticity, ownership validation, in-
tegrity, and non-repudiation. In Bitcoin, Ethereum, and other
public blockchains, signatures authorize asset transfers and
bind transactions to the corresponding signing keys [17],
[18]. In permissioned blockchains, signatures additionally
support participant authentication, access control, endorse-
ment collection, and policy enforcement [1]. Therefore, the
migration from classical signatures to post-quantum digital
signatures is a critical issue for the future resilience of

Several surveys have analyzed the implications of quantum
computing and PQC for blockchain systems. Yang et al.
provide a comprehensive survey and comparison of post-
quantum and quantum blockchains, highlighting the cryp-
tographic challenges that arise when blockchain systems
rely on quantum-vulnerable primitives [19]. Buser et al. fur-
ther extend this perspective by surveying post-quantum ex-
otic signatures for blockchain applications, including multi-
signatures, aggregate signatures, threshold signatures, adap-
tor signatures, blind signatures, and ring signatures [20].
Their work demonstrates that post-quantum migration in
blockchain is not limited to replacing ECDSA with an or-
dinary post-quantum signature. Instead, it also affects ad-
vanced blockchain functionalities such as account manage-
ment, consensus efficiency, privacy-preserving transactions,
atomic swaps, payment channels, and scriptless blockchain
protocols.
Beyond survey studies, several works have investigated
post-quantum signatures in blockchain-oriented settings.
Schemitt et al. assessed the impact of post-quantum dig-
ital signature algorithms on blockchains by benchmarking
schemes such as ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, Falcon, and re-
lated candidates [21]. Their results suggest that some post-
quantum signatures can be computationally feasible for
blockchain verification workloads. However, their evalua-
tion is mainly based on cryptographic benchmarking and
blockchain simulation rather than a deployed Hyperledger
Fabric network. Similarly, primitive-level PQC benchmark-
ing studies, such as the work of Algar-Fernandez et al.,
compare multiple post-quantum KEMs and digital signatures
on commodity CPUs and report favorable performance for
lattice-based schemes such as Kyber and Dilithium/ML-DSA
[22]. Xu et al. proposed a post-quantum blockchain transac-
tion model based on Dilithium, focusing on the use of lattice-
based signatures for transaction authentication and scalability
analysis [23]. However, this work does not evaluate Hyper-
ledger Fabric or Fabric-specific endorsement, ordering, and
validation mechanisms.
Such studies are useful for understanding primitive-level
cost, but they do not capture blockchain-specific phenomena
such as endorsement latency, ordering behavior, block-size
growth, ledger storage, peer validation overhead, or resource
consumption.
Other works propose alternative post-quantum signature
constructions for distributed ledgers. Shahid and Khan pro-
posed Smart Digital Signatures, a hash-based post-quantum
digital signature scheme designed for distributed ledgers
[24]. Earlier works also explored anti-quantum authen-
tication models and lattice-based transaction authentica-
tion mechanisms for blockchain systems [25]. In addition,
privacy-oriented approaches such as MatRiCT investigated
lattice-based post-quantum confidential transactions [26].
These contributions are important because they demonstrate
the diversity of post-quantum blockchain signature research.
Nevertheless, most of them either focus on new crypto-
graphic constructions, public blockchain models, privacy-
preserving transactions, or simulation-level evaluation. They
do not provide a systematic empirical assessment of post-
quantum or hybrid signatures in a permissioned Hyperledger
Fabric deployment.
These observations motivate the need for system-level
evaluation of post-quantum signatures in permissioned Fab-
ric networks, as discussed further in Section II-E.

FABRIC INTEGRATION
Hyperledger Fabric is one of the most widely used permis-
sioned blockchain platforms for enterprise applications. Its
modular architecture, membership-based identity model, en-
dorsement policies, and configurable ordering service make
it attractive for consortium and institutional deployments [1].
However, these same characteristics also make post-quantum
migration more complex than in simpler transaction-signing
models. In Fabric, cryptographic mechanisms are involved in
client authentication, X.509 certificates, membership service
providers, endorsement signatures, transaction envelopes,
TLS channels, and block validation. Therefore, integrating
post-quantum signatures into Fabric requires careful con-
sideration of both cryptographic compatibility and system
performance.
PQFabric is one of the closest and most important works
addressing post-quantum Hyperledger Fabric integration [8].
It investigates how Fabric can be modified to support post-
quantum cryptographic mechanisms and quantum-resistant
identities. This work is significant because it directly targets
Fabric rather than generic blockchain systems. However,
its approach involves modifications to Fabric cryptographic
components, which may affect compatibility, maintainabil-
ity, and deployment complexity. Moreover, while PQFabric
demonstrates the feasibility of post-quantum integration, it
does not fully address the broader system-level benchmark-
ing dimensions required for practical migration planning,
such as payload-size sensitivity, resource monitoring, block-
size overhead, and statistical validation under controlled
workloads.
More recently, Abbas et al. investigated quantum-safe
blockchain integration in Hyperledger Fabric by modify-
ing certificate-generation mechanisms and evaluating post-
quantum schemes using tools such as Hyperledger Caliper
and Prometheus [9]. Their work is highly relevant because
it combines Hyperledger Fabric, post-quantum cryptography,
performance evaluation, and monitoring. Nevertheless, sev-
eral aspects remain open. First, Abbas et al. evaluate Kyber,
which is a key encapsulation mechanism rather than a dig-
ital signature scheme, alongside Dilithium and Falcon. This
requires a clear distinction between key establishment and
transaction authentication. Second, existing evaluations often
provide limited detail about topology, endorsement poli-
cies, workload configuration, payload variation, repetitions,
confidence intervals, and transaction-level overhead. Third,

D. HYPERLEDGER FABRIC PERFORMANCE
BENCHMARKING
A rigorous evaluation of post-quantum signatures in Hyper-
ledger Fabric must be grounded in the broader literature on
Fabric performance benchmarking. Fabric performance is not
determined only by cryptographic operations. It depends on
the execute–order–validate architecture, endorsement poli-
cies, ordering configuration, block size, batch timeout, state
database, workload characteristics, peer topology, and avail-
able resources [1]. Therefore, any evaluation of post-quantum
overhead must control these parameters to avoid attribut-
ing configuration-induced performance differences to cryp-

Fabric performance benchmarking. Fabric performance is not
determined only by cryptographic operations. It depends on
the execute–order–validate architecture, endorsement poli-
cies, ordering configuration, block size, batch timeout, state
database, workload characteristics, peer topology, and avail-
able resources [1]. Therefore, any evaluation of post-quantum
overhead must control these parameters to avoid attribut-
ing configuration-induced performance differences to cryp-
tographic changes.
Androulaki et al. introduced Hyperledger Fabric as a mod-
ular permissioned blockchain architecture based on execute–
order–validate transaction processing [1]. In this architecture,
clients first submit transaction proposals to endorsing peers.
Endorsed transactions are then ordered into blocks by the
ordering service, and peers subsequently validate and com-
mit the blocks to the ledger. Fabric documentation further
clarifies this transaction flow and the role of endorsement,
ordering, validation, and commit phases [30]. Manevich et
al. analyze endorsement in Fabric through service discovery,
showing how endorsement selection and transaction routing
affect transaction processing [31]. These studies are impor-
tant for post-quantum evaluation because digital signatures
may affect several stages of the Fabric pipeline, including
proposal authentication, endorsement collection, transaction
envelope size, validation, and block dissemination.
Consensus and ordering configuration also influence per-
formance. Fabric deployments commonly use Raft-based
ordering services, whose underlying consensus principles
are described by Ongaro and Ousterhout [32]. While Raft
itself is not a post-quantum mechanism, the ordering layer
can be affected indirectly by larger transaction payloads and
increased block sizes caused by post-quantum signatures.
Therefore, PQC benchmarking in Fabric must clearly report
the number of orderers, batch size, batch timeout, and block-
formation parameters.
Several empirical and analytical studies have shown that
Fabric performance is highly configuration-sensitive. Nasir
et al. provided an early performance analysis of Hyperledger
Fabric, examining latency, throughput, and scalability under
different settings [33]. More recent studies provide deeper
insights into workload design and resource behavior. Wang et
al. proposed BlockLoader, a Hyperledger Fabric evaluation
framework that extends Caliper-based benchmarking with
realistic workload patterns such as uniform, linear, random,
burst, single-peak, multi-peak, and dynamic workloads [34].
Their work shows that workload shape, endorsement policy
breadth, endorsement policy depth, node failures, and recov-
eries significantly influence throughput, latency, CPU usage,
and memory usage.
Other studies emphasize the impact of Fabric configuration
parameters such as block size, timeout, and commit capacity.
Melo et al. model Fabric performance using stochastic Petri
nets and show that block size, batch timeout, arrival rate,
and commit capacity can substantially affect mean response
time and throughput [35]. Lechhab Ouadrassi et al. empiri-
cally demonstrated that endorsement policy, block size, and
peer count significantly affect Fabric latency and through-
put [36], motivating the need to control these parameters
when evaluating cryptographic changes. For example, OR
endorsement policies generally provide lower latency and
higher throughput than stricter AND policies, while block
size and timeout determine the latency–throughput trade-off.
These findings are essential for PQC benchmarking because
post-quantum signatures may increase transaction size and
validation cost, and their effect may interact with Fabric
batching and endorsement behavior.

Table 1 summarizes the coverage of eleven evaluation dimen-
sions across the reviewed studies. The comparison confirms

Fabric.
The reviewed literature reveals three main research
streams. The first stream focuses on quantum threats, post-
quantum cryptographic standardization, and hybrid migra-
tion strategies. This stream establishes the need to migrate
from ECDSA toward standardized post-quantum digital sig-
natures such as ML-DSA/Dilithium [2]–[4], [13]. The sec-
ond stream investigates post-quantum signatures and post-
quantum architectures for blockchain systems. These works
show that blockchain platforms must prepare for quantum
threats and that PQC affects transaction authentication, ac-
count management, consensus efficiency, and privacy [19]–

from ECDSA toward standardized post-quantum digital sig-
natures such as ML-DSA/Dilithium [2]–[4], [13]. The sec-
ond stream investigates post-quantum signatures and post-
quantum architectures for blockchain systems. These works
show that blockchain platforms must prepare for quantum
threats and that PQC affects transaction authentication, ac-
count management, consensus efficiency, and privacy [19]–
[21]. The third stream examines Hyperledger Fabric per-
formance, showing that throughput, latency, and resource
consumption depend strongly on endorsement policies, block
parameters, workload patterns, ordering configuration, and
peer capacity [1], [31], [33]–[36].
Despite these advances, a significant gap remains at the
intersection of post-quantum digital signatures and Hyper-
ledger Fabric performance evaluation. Existing PQC bench-
marks often evaluate cryptographic primitives in isolation,
TLS settings, or blockchain simulations. Such evaluations
are valuable, but they do not capture the complete Fabric
transaction pipeline, including endorsement, ordering, val-
idation, block formation, and ledger commit. Conversely,
existing Fabric performance studies provide detailed insights
into configuration tuning and benchmarking methodology,
but they do not evaluate post-quantum or hybrid signatures.
Finally, the few Fabric-oriented PQC studies either modify
Fabric internals, focus on certificate generation, rely on sim-
ulation, or provide limited analysis of payload variability,
block-size overhead, resource consumption, and statistical
confidence.
This gap motivates the present work. Unlike primitive-
level PQC benchmarks, the proposed study evaluates the
impact of post-quantum and hybrid signatures in a deployed
Hyperledger Fabric network. Unlike general Fabric bench-
marking studies, it focuses specifically on the cryptographic
migration from ECDSA toward ML-DSA and hybrid sig-
nature configurations. The evaluation considers blockchain-
specific metrics, including transaction throughput, latency,
success rate, CPU consumption, memory usage, block-size
overhead, and payload-size sensitivity. This system-level per-
spective is necessary because the practical feasibility of post-
quantum migration in Fabric cannot be inferred from isolated
signing and verification timings alone.
More specifically, this work positions itself as a controlled
empirical benchmark of hybrid post-quantum signatures in
Hyperledger Fabric. By keeping Fabric topology, endorse-
ment policy, ordering configuration, workload parameters,
and payload scenarios consistent across experiments, the
study aims to isolate the performance impact of the cryp-
tographic transition. By measuring both performance and
resource indicators, it further investigates whether the main
overhead of PQC integration arises from cryptographic com-
putation, increased transaction size, block growth, validation
cost, or peer/orderer resource consumption.
Therefore, the contribution of this work is twofold. First,
it provides empirical evidence on the feasibility and cost of
integrating ML-DSA and hybrid signatures into a Fabric-
oriented transaction workflow. Second, it bridges the gap
between post-quantum cryptographic benchmarking and per-
missioned blockchain performance analysis. This contribu-
tion is important for organizations planning quantum-safe
migration in enterprise blockchain infrastructures, where se-
curity, compatibility, throughput, latency, storage overhead,
and operational cost must be evaluated jointly.
III. BACKGROUND AND PRELIMINARIES
This section provides the technical foundations necessary for
understanding the proposed hybrid post-quantum signature
evaluation. Section III-A describes the Hyperledger Fabric
transaction pipeline and identifies where digital signatures
intervene. Section III-B compares the two signature schemes
used in this work: ECDSA and ML-DSA-65. Section III-C
presents the hybrid signature migration model and explains
the architectural rationale for application-layer integration.
A. HYPERLEDGER FABRIC TRANSACTION PIPELINE
Hyperledger Fabric processes transactions through a three-
phase pipeline known as execute–order–validate [1]. Under-
standing this pipeline is essential for identifying where digital
signatures appear and where post-quantum overhead may
arise.
In theexecution phase, a client application constructs
a transaction proposal containing the function name, ar-
guments, and a digital signature authenticating the client
identity. The proposal is sent to a set of endorsing peers
determined by the channel’s endorsement policy. Each en-
dorser independently executes the chaincode (smart contract)
against its local copy of the world state, produces a read-
write set representing the proposed state changes, and signs
the result with its own ECDSA key. The endorsed responses
are returned to the client, which assembles them into a
transaction envelope.

In theordering phase, the client submits the assem-
bled transaction envelope to the ordering service. In Fab-
ric 2.5, the ordering service typically uses the Raft consen-
sus protocol [32]. The orderers group incoming transactions
into blocks according to configurable batching parameters:
MaxMessageCount(maximum number of transactions
per block) andBatchTimeout(maximum time before a
block is cut). The resulting blocks are distributed to all peers
on the channel.
In thevalidation phase, each peer validates every transac-
tion in the received block. Validation includes verifying en-
dorsement signatures against the endorsement policy, check-
ing read-write set conflicts (MVCC validation), and verifying
the transaction envelope signature. Valid transactions update
the world state; invalid transactions are marked but still
recorded in the immutable ledger. The block, including all
transaction envelopes and their signatures, is then appended
to the peer’s local ledger.
Digital signatures are therefore involved at multiple stages
of this pipeline: client proposal authentication, endorsement
signing, transaction envelope construction, and block-level
validation. Consequently, any increase in signature size di-
rectly affects the transaction envelope, block payload, ledger
storage, and network propagation cost. However, the com-
putational cost of signature generation and verification rep-
resents only one component of the end-to-end transaction
latency; endorsement collection, ordering, block formation,
MVCC validation, and state-database commit also contribute
significantly. This observation motivates the need to evaluate
post-quantum signature overhead at the system level rather
than through isolated cryptographic benchmarks.

ECDSA.The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm
over the P-256 curve is the default signature mechanism
in Hyperledger Fabric. It is used for client identity au-
thentication, endorsement signing, and transaction envelope
validation through Fabric’s Membership Service Provider
(MSP) and Blockchain Crypto Service Provider (BCCSP)
[3]. ECDSA signatures are compact, typically around 70–
72 bytes in DER encoding, and computationally efficient on
modern hardware. However, ECDSA relies on the hardness
of the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDLP),
which is vulnerable to Shor’s algorithm on a sufficiently
powerful quantum computer [2].
ML-DSA-65.ML-DSA-65 is the Module-Lattice-Based
Digital Signature Algorithm parameter set corresponding
to NIST security-strength category 3 in FIPS 204 [4]. It
is the standardized successor of CRYSTALS-Dilithium 3
from the NIST post-quantum cryptography standardization
process [13]. ML-DSA relies on module-lattice hardness
assumptions, mainly Module-LWE and Module-SIS [11]. Its
signatures have a fixed size for a given parameter set: 3,309
bytes for ML-DSA-65, independent of the message length.
In the default FIPS 204 signing procedure, ML-DSA uses a
hedged variant with fresh randomness, while a deterministic
variant is also specified. This fixed artifact size is important
for blockchain applications because it makes the signature
contribution to transaction and block size predictable. How-
ever, the signature size is approximately 47×larger than an
ECDSA DER-encoded signature, which may affect transac-
tion envelope size, block payload, and ledger growth.
The choice of ML-DSA-65 as the primary parameter set
in this work reflects an intermediate security–storage trade-
off among the three FIPS 204 configurations. ML-DSA-44
provides security-strength category 2 with the smallest signa-
ture and public-key artifacts, whereas ML-DSA-87 provides
category 5 with the largest artifacts. ML-DSA-65 occupies
the intermediate category 3 position, with a 3,309-byte sig-
nature and a 1,952-byte public key. In addition to the primary
ML-DSA-65 evaluation, Section VI reports a targeted exper-
imental comparison of ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-
DSA-87 to quantify the corresponding signing-performance
and storage trade-offs.

ahybridsignature model rather than a full replacement of
Fabric’s native cryptographic layer. This subsection explains
the rationale and implications of this choice.
Approach.This work does not replace the native Fab-
ric ECDSA mechanism. Instead, Fabric continues to use
ECDSA for its standard identity management, endorsement
signing, and transaction validation pipeline. ML-DSA-65 is
added at theapplication layerthrough a dedicated PQC
signing microservice invoked by the client application be-

flow, the application-level ML-DSA-65 signature is per-
sisted through the chaincode data model, while Fabric-native

This approach differs fundamentally from works such as

The application-layer approach adopted here preserves full

Rationale.The hybrid model is motivated by three consid-

1)Backward compatibility.Existing Fabric infrastructure—
including MSP configuration, X.509 certificates, TLS
channels, peer binaries, and SDK clients—remains
unchanged. This reduces deployment risk and allows
incremental migration.
2)Defense in depth.During the migration period, the
system benefits from both classical and post-quantum
protection. If a vulnerability is discovered in ML-DSA,
the ECDSA layer still provides classical security. Con-
versely, if a quantum computer threatens ECDSA, the
ML-DSA-65 signature provides post-quantum authenti-
cation.
3)Separation of concerns.The post-quantum signing logic
is isolated in a dedicated microservice, which can be
independently scaled and updated as PQC standards

Scope and limitations.The hybrid model provides
application-level cryptographic evidence for transaction au-
thenticity and document integrity. However, it does not mod-
ify Fabric’s internal cryptographic operations. Specifically,
the following Fabric components remain protected only by
classical ECDSA:
•MSP identity certificates and enrollment;
•TLS channels between peers, orderers, and clients;
•endorsement signatures produced by peers;
•block-level metadata signatures;
•ordering-service consensus messages.
Full quantum resistance of the Fabric infrastructure would
require modifications to the BCCSP, MSP, and TLS layers,
which is beyond the scope of this work and is identified as
a direction for future research. The present study focuses on
evaluating the performance impact of hybrid post-quantum
signatures at the application and transaction level, where the
overhead is measurable through standard blockchain bench-
marking tools.
Migration-depth comparison.The proposed architec-
ture represents an incremental application-layer migration
strategy and therefore has a narrower quantum-resistance
scope than approaches that modify Fabric’s credential or
cryptographic infrastructure. Abbas et al. [9] introduce
post-quantum key material through modifications to the
credential-generation/X.509 process, requiring changes to
organizational credential provisioning. PQFabric [8] adopts
a deeper integration point by modifying Fabric cryptographic
and credential-processing components, including the BCCSP
and MSP. In contrast, the present approach leaves Fabric
core binaries, MSP configuration, TLS, and endorsement
mechanisms unchanged in the evaluated deployment and
confines PQC integration to the application signing service,
PQ-key registration, and chaincode workflow. This reduces
the depth of software and credential migration but leaves
Fabric’s infrastructure-level cryptographic mechanisms clas-
sical. A full-stack migration would additionally require post-
quantum protection of identity and credential management,
peer endorsements, TLS and inter-node communications,
ordering-service cryptography, and client-side authentication
and signing. These approaches should therefore be under-
stood as different points on a protection-versus-integration
spectrum rather than as functionally equivalent alternatives.

IV . SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND DESIGN
This section describes the architecture of the proposed hybrid
post-quantum signature system deployed on Hyperledger
Fabric. Section IV-A presents the overall system topology
and component roles. Section IV-B details the hybrid sig-
nature workflow for document creation and signing. Sec-
tion IV-C describes the chaincode design and on-ledger data
model. Section IV-D presents the PQC signing microservice.
Section IV-E summarizes the implementation considerations
required to ensure deterministic execution, avoid concur-
rency conflicts, and satisfy the endorsement policy.
A. SYSTEM OVERVIEW
The proposed system consists of three main layers: (i) a
Hyperledger Fabric network providing the permissioned
blockchain infrastructure, (ii) a post-quantum signing mi-
croservice providing ML-DSA-65 cryptographic operations,
and (iii) client applications that orchestrate the hybrid signa-
ture workflow. Fig. 1 illustrates the overall architecture.
The Fabric network is configured as a multi-organization
consortium with the following topology:
•Peers:Four endorsing peers distributed across
two organizations—peer1-org1,peer2-org1
(Org1MSP) andpeer1-org2,peer2-org2
(Org2MSP). Each peer maintains a local copy of the
ledger and a CouchDB state database instance.
•Ordering service:Three Raft-based orderers
(orderer1,orderer2,orderer3) providing
crash fault-tolerant consensus.
•Endorsement policy:MAJORITY , requiring endorse-
ment from a majority of channel member organizations.
In the two-organization configuration used in this work,
this requires endorsements from both Org1MSP and
Org2MSP, i.e., at least one peer from each organiza-
tion.This policy is stricter than a single-organization
policy and reflects realistic multi-party governance sce-
narios.
•Channel:A single application channel
(tokenchannel) is used for all transactions.

Chaincode-as-a-Service (CCAAS) model, where the chain-
code logic runs in a dedicated container external to the

B. HYBRID SIGNATURE WORKFLOW
The hybrid signature workflow combines Fabric-native
ECDSA operations with application-level ML-DSA-65 sign-
ing. Two primary transaction types are supported: document
creation and document signing. Both workflows follow the
same architectural principle: the PQC signing step occurs at
the client side before transaction submission, while the Fabric
endorsement and validation pipeline operates with its native
ECDSA mechanism.

document creation by computing a cryptographic hash of
the document content and invoking the PQC microservice
to generate an ML-DSA-65 signature over this hash before
transaction submission. The generated signature is not per-
sisted in the ledger state; the chaincode registers the docu-
ment metadata and initializes an empty signature collection.
The transaction is then endorsed, ordered, and committed
using Fabric’s native ECDSA-based mechanisms.

an ML-DSA-65 signature through theSignDocument

D. PQC SIGNING MICROSERVICE
The post-quantum signing operations are provided by a
dedicated microservice external to the Fabric network.
This design isolates the PQC cryptographic logic from the
blockchain infrastructure and allows the signing component
to be updated, scaled, or replaced independently from the
Fabric peers and orderers.
The microservice is implemented as a Python FastAPI ap-
plication using theliboqs-pythonlibrary version 0.14.1.
It exposes a REST endpoint,POST /pqc/sign, which
receives a message or content hash, signs it using a persistent
ML-DSA-65 private key, and returns the Base64-encoded
signature, the Base64-encoded public key, and the measured
signing time. The ML-DSA-65 key pair is generated once at
service initialization and persisted to disk, ensuring that the
same public key is used across signing operations within a
deployment session.
For the functionally equivalent classical baseline, the ex-
ternal signing service was additionally configured to gen-
erate application-layer ECDSA P-256 signatures over the
same document content hash used by the ML-DSA-65 work-
flow. The ECDSA signing path follows the same client-
to-service interaction and returns the signature, public-key
representation, and signing metadata for submission through
the sameSignDocumenttransaction workflow. This addi-
tional path is used only as an experimental control to isolate
the storage cost associated with the application-layer signa-
ture scheme. The measured ECDSA P-256 artifacts consist

E. IMPLEMENTATION CONSIDERATIONS
The deployment of hybrid post-quantum signatures in a
multi-organization Fabric network required several imple-
mentation safeguards to preserve deterministic execution,
avoid concurrency conflicts, and satisfy the endorsement
policy.
First, all chaincode-generated timestamps were derived
from Fabric’s deterministic transaction timestamp using
GetTxTimestamp()rather than from local wall-clock
time. This is necessary because endorsing peers execute the
same chaincode independently, and any non-deterministic
value may produce divergent read-write sets and endorse-
ment mismatches.
Second, the benchmark workload was designed to avoid
artificial MVCC conflicts by assigning each Caliper worker
a dedicated set of document identifiers. This prevents multi-
ple workers from concurrently updating the same document
state while preserving the semantics of theSignDocument
transaction.
Third, service discovery was enabled in the Caliper net-
work configuration to ensure that transaction proposals are
sent to endorsing peers across both organizations. This is
required to satisfy the MAJORITY endorsement policy used
in the evaluated Fabric network.
These implementation considerations are particularly rel-
evant for hybrid PQC deployments because they combine
off-chain cryptographic services with deterministic on-chain
execution. They ensure that the measured performance re-
flects the cost of the hybrid signature workflow rather than
avoidable deployment errors.

2) Workload Design
Four workload modules were implemented to evaluate the
two transaction types (CreateDocument and SignDocument)
under two cryptographic configurations (ECDSA baseline
and PQC hybrid):
1)CreateDocument–PQC: generates a unique document
identifier and prepares acontentHashargument. In
the baseline scenarios, this argument is a SHA-256
hex-encoded digest. In the payload-robustness scenario,
the same argument is used as a controlled hexadeci-
mal payload carrier rather than as a semantic crypto-
graphic hash. Before transaction submission, the work-
load invokes the PQC microservice to generate an
ML-DSA-65 signature over the prepared content hash.
The generated signature and public key are not passed
toCreateDocumentas transaction arguments; the
chaincode registers the document metadata and initial-
izes an empty signature collection.
2)CreateDocument–ECDSA: identical logic to the PQC
variant, but without invoking the PQC microservice. A
synthetic delay of 2.44 ms is injected to equalize the
architectural overhead introduced by the HTTP round-
trip to the microservice. This delay value corresponds to
the measured average latency of the PQC microservice
at unit concurrency (n= 100measurements, mean=
2.44ms, range= [1,30]ms).
3)SignDocument–PQC: each worker first creates a dedi-
cated pool of documents during the initialization phase,
then submitsSignDocumenttransactions that invoke
the PQC microservice and append ML-DSA-65 signa-
tures. Each document receives at most one signature to
avoidMVCC_READ_CONFLICTerrors.
4)SignDocument–ECDSA: identical structure to the
PQC variant, with synthetic delay replacing the mi-
croservice invocation.
Each workload generates unique document identifiers in-
corporating the worker index, round index, and a run-specific
timestamp to prevent cross-worker contention and ensure that
successive benchmark runs operate on independent ledger
state.
3) ECDSA Baseline Design Rationale
A key methodological consideration is the design of a fair
ECDSA baseline. In the PQC hybrid workflow, the client
application performs an additional HTTP round-trip to the
PQC microservice before submitting the transaction to Fab-
ric. If the ECDSA baseline omits this step entirely, any
observed performance difference may reflect the HTTP over-
head rather than the cryptographic cost of ML-DSA-65.
Conversely, the ECDSA baseline should not include ML-
DSA-65 signing, as the goal is to isolate the impact of the
post-quantum signature.
The adopted solution injects a calibrated synthetic delay
(2.44 ms) into the ECDSA workload to match the mea-
sured average HTTP round-trip latency of the PQC mi-
croservice. This approach provides comparable client-side
preparation overhead between the two configurations. For
SignDocument, the Fabric-side comparison additionally
captures the impact of transmitting and storing the larger ML-
DSA-65 signature artifacts, whereasCreateDocument
does not persist these artifacts. The validity of this calibration
is supported by the microservice latency characterization
reported in Section VI-A, which showed that the HTTP
latency is payload-size invariant and averages 2.1–2.8 ms at
unit concurrency. The ECDSA configuration should therefore
be interpreted as a latency-matched Fabric baseline rather
than a pure no-delay Fabric baseline.

D. PERFORMANCE METRICS
The following metrics are collected and reported for each
experimental scenario:
1)Transaction throughput (TPS): the number of suc-
cessfully committed transactions per second, computed
as the total number of successful transactions divided
by the elapsed time between the first and last committed
transaction.
2)Average latency (s): the arithmetic mean of the per-
transaction latency, where latency is defined as the time
elapsed from transaction submission to transaction com-
mit confirmation, as measured by Caliper.
3)Maximum and minimum latency (s): the extreme
latency values observed across all transactions in a run,
providing information about tail behavior and best-case
performance.
4)Transaction success and failure counts: the number
of transactions that committed successfully versus those
that failed due to endorsement errors, MVCC conflicts,
timeouts, or other Fabric-level rejections.
5)Send rate (TPS): the actual rate at which Caliper sub-
mitted transaction proposals, which may differ from the
configured target rate under high load due to backpres-
sure.

4) Rationale for Sample Sizes
The choice of sample sizes reflects a trade-off between sta-
tistical rigor and experimental cost:
•n=30for the primary benchmarks (S1, S2): provides a
reasonable basis for normal-approximation inference on
the sample mean, yields narrower confidence intervals,
and improves the ability to detect moderate effect sizes.
•n=5for stress tests (S3, S4) and resource monitoring
(S6): each run involves substantial setup time (document
pool creation) and execution time;n= 5provides
meaningful variance estimates while remaining practi-
cally feasible.
•n=5 per conditionfor the supplementary targeted
experiments: the ML-DSA parameter-set comparison
and the two-instance signing-service evaluation. For
the multi-instance experiment, five independent runs
were performed at each target submission rate (10 and
50 TPS), providing repeated observations for estimating
mean performance, 95% confidence intervals, and run-
to-run variability while keeping the additional experi-
mental cost manageable.
•n=9–10for payload robustness (S5): a compromise
between the primary benchmarks and the stress tests,
sufficient to apply the Welch t-test with reasonable
statistical power.
This multi-tier sampling strategy ensures that the most crit-
ical comparisons (baseline throughput and latency) receive
the highest statistical rigor, while secondary analyses (stress
behavior, resource consumption, payload sensitivity) are still
supported by repeated measurements and formal hypothesis
testing rather than single-run observations.

I. SUMMARY OF RESULTS
Table 18 consolidates the key results across all evaluated
dimensions.
The results show that, under the tested single-host
Fabric deployment and workload conditions, no statisti-
cally significant degradation was detected in the primary
transaction-level performance metrics of the hybrid ML-
DSA-65/ECDSA configuration relative to the ECDSA base-
line. The primary throughput and average-latency compar-
isons further exhibit small-to-negligible Cohen’sdeffect
sizes. Exploratory TOST sensitivity analysis supports the
±10%equivalence criterion for the two primary throughput
comparisons, whereas the corresponding latency compar-
isons do not satisfy this strict equivalence margin because
of their wider confidence intervals. Accordingly, the revised
analysis distinguishes absence of a statistically significant
difference from formal statistical equivalence.
The only practically and statistically significant difference
observed in the evaluation is the on-ledger block-size over-
head. PQC hybrid blocks are 1.48×larger than ECDSA
baseline blocks (p <0.05), which is a direct and expected
consequence of storing the larger ML-DSA-65 signature and
public-key artifacts in the Fabric ledger.
These findings suggest that, for organizations planning
post-quantum migration in enterprise Hyperledger Fabric
deployments, the primary operational cost of adopting hybrid
ML-DSA-65/ECDSA signatures is ledger storage growth
rather than transaction processing overhead.
VII. DISCUSSION
This section interprets the experimental results in the context
of the research objectives, analyzes the architectural trade-
offs of the proposed hybrid signature scheme, examines the
broader implications for post-quantum migration in enter-
prise blockchain systems, and identifies the threats to validity
of the evaluation.
A. PERFORMANCE TRANSP ARENCY OF HYBRID
ML-DSA-65 SIGNATURES
The central finding of this evaluation is that the hybrid ML-
DSA-65/ECDSA signature scheme introduces no statistically
significant overhead on the primary transaction-level perfor-
mance metrics under the tested Hyperledger Fabric deploy-
ment. This result holds across the evaluated transaction types,
submission rates, payload sizes, and resource-consumption
measurements. The only practically meaningful statistically
significant difference is observed at the ledger-storage level,
where PQC hybrid blocks are larger due to the storage of
ML-DSA-65 signature and public-key artifacts.

The absence of measurable transaction-level overhead can
be explained by the interplay between three factors. First,
the cryptographic computation time for ML-DSA-65 signing
is negligible at the system level. TheliboqsC-optimized
implementation reduces per-signature latency to 0.226 ms,
which represents less than 0.05% of the average Fabric
commit latency under the tested workload. Even at the high-
est concurrency tested (20 concurrent requests), the PQC
microservice response time remains below 22 ms, which is
still a small fraction of Fabric’s endorsement and ordering
pipeline. Second, the execute–order–validate architecture of
Hyperledger Fabric serializes the cryptographic overhead
with the network-bound operations of endorsement collec-
tion, Raft consensus, and block propagation, all of which
dominate the transaction lifecycle. The additional latency
introduced by the PQC signing step is effectively masked by
these pipeline stages. Third, the ML-DSA-65 signing time is
effectively insensitive to payload size within the tested range,
as the algorithm internally hashes the input before signing
regardless of message length. This behavior explains why the
performance transparency observed with the baseline pay-
load representation (64 hexadecimal characters for a SHA-
256 digest) also extends to larger transaction arguments of
1 KB and 10 KB in the payload robustness evaluation.
These observations suggest that the barrier to adopting
post-quantum signatures in Hyperledger Fabric is not com-
putational cost but rather architectural integration complexity
and on-ledger storage overhead.
B. BLOCK-SIZE OVERHEAD AS THE PRIMARY
TRADE-OFF
The principal storage-related difference observed in the
original evaluation is the 1.48×block-size overhead of
the PQC hybrid configuration for the signing-intensive
SignDocumentworkload (t= 6.422,p <0.05). This
overhead arises directly from the on-ledger storage of ML-
DSA-65 signature artifacts: eachSignDocumenttransac-
tion stores a 3,309-byte signature and a 1,952-byte public
key, which after Base64 encoding total approximately 7,016
characters per signing event. This ratio is therefore specific to
transactions that persist post-quantum signature material and
should not be interpreted as a uniform storage multiplier for
all transaction types.
The storage results illustrate the distinction between
cryptographic-artifact expansion and complete Fabric block
expansion. Although the encoded ML-DSA-65 signature and
public-key artifacts are approximately 20.9×larger than
the corresponding application-layer ECDSA P-256 artifacts,
the observed active-block size increases by approximately
1.43×. This difference arises because the application-layer
signature artifacts represent only part of the serialized Fab-
ric transaction. Endorsement information, MSP credentials,
transaction metadata, read-write sets, block headers, and
other common protocol structures contribute substantial stor-
age in both configurations and therefore dilute the relative
effect of the larger ML-DSA-65 artifacts at the block level.
From a practical perspective, the functionally equiva-
lent comparison indicates that signing-intensive workloads
should anticipate an active-block storage increase of approx-
imately 1.43×relative to an application-layer ECDSA P-
256 workflow under the evaluated conditions. The previously
reported 1.48×ratio remains relevant as the total increase rel-
ative to the original latency-matched Fabric baseline without
application-layer signature storage. These two ratios there-
fore answer different questions and should not be interpreted
interchangeably.

C. ARCHITECTURAL TRADE-OFFS
The application-layer integration approach adopted in this
work represents a deliberate trade-off between migration
intrusiveness and quantum-resistance coverage. By limiting
PQC integration to the application workflow, the architec-
ture avoids modifications to Fabric’s native cryptographic
infrastructure, but consequently provides a narrower post-
quantum protection boundary than approaches that modify
the credential or cryptographic layers.
Comparison with Fabric-internal modification.Ap-
proaches such as PQFabric [8] integrate post-quantum
mechanisms more deeply into Fabric’s cryptographic and
credential-processing stack, including components such as
the BCCSP and MSP. Such integration extends post-quantum
protection beyond the application layer but requires com-
patible cryptographic software and credential changes across
the affected Fabric components. In contrast, the architecture
evaluated in this work leaves Fabric core binaries and na-
tive endorsement, MSP, and TLS mechanisms unchanged.
The corresponding benefit is reduced migration depth and
independent evolution of the external PQC component; the
corresponding limitation is that infrastructure-level Fabric
cryptography remains classical.
Comparison with credential-level modification.Abbas
et al. [9] adopt a deeper identity-oriented integration by incor-
porating post-quantum key material through modifications to
the credential-generation/X.509 process. This extends PQC
integration into the organizational credential layer but re-
quires corresponding changes to credential provisioning. The
present architecture does not modify Fabric’s X.509 or MSP
credential structure; instead, the ML-DSA-65 key is asso-
ciated with the authenticated MSP organization through the
application-layer PQC key registry. This reduces credential-
migration requirements, but it does not provide post-quantum
protection for the native Fabric identity infrastructure.
Protection-versus-integration trade-off.As discussed in
Section III-C, the compared approaches represent different
migration depths rather than functionally equivalent security
solutions. The present architecture occupies the application-
layer end of this spectrum, with limited modification require-
ments but limited quantum-resistance coverage. Deeper cryp-
tographic or credential-level approaches extend protection
into additional Fabric components at the cost of broader soft-
ware, identity, and credential migration. A full-stack post-
quantum migration would require protection of the remaining
quantum-vulnerable mechanisms, including identity and cre-
dential management, peer endorsements, TLS and inter-node
communications, ordering-service cryptography, and client-
side authentication and signing. The proposed architecture
should therefore be evaluated as an incremental migration
step rather than as a substitute for such a full-stack recon-
struction.
MSP-authenticated application-layer key binding.
Although the proposed architecture leaves Fabric’s na-
tive identity and cryptographic infrastructure unchanged,
it enforces an application-layer association between
each participating organization and its authorized ML-
DSA-65 public key. This association is implemented
through an on-chain PQC key registry. During key reg-
istration, the organization identifier is derived directly
from the caller’s authenticated Fabric identity using
ctx.GetClientIdentity().GetMSPID(), rather
than being supplied as a transaction argument. During
SignDocument(), the chaincode requires anACTIVE
PQCKeyRecordfor the authenticated organization and
accepts the submitted ML-DSA-65 public key only if it
matches the organization’s registered key. Consequently, an
authenticated participant cannot arbitrarily associate an un-
registered, revoked, or mismatched ML-DSA-65 public key
with a signing transaction. This binding is achieved without
modifying Fabric’s native MSP, BCCSP, X.509 credential
structure, TLS configuration, or endorsement mechanism.
Trade-off: off-chain ML-DSA verification.The MSP-to-
PQC key binding is enforced at the application layer rather
than being incorporated directly into Fabric’s credential in-
frastructure. Although the chaincode verifies that the ML-
DSA-65 public key associated with a signing transaction
matches the active key registered for the MSP-authenticated
organization, it does not execute the ML-DSA-65 verification
algorithm during transaction processing. Cryptographic veri-

Limitation: partial quantum resistance.The primary
security limitation of the proposed architecture is that
post-quantum protection is confined to the application-
level ML-DSA-65 signature evidence. Fabric’s native
MSP/X.509 identities, peer endorsement signatures, TLS-
protected communications, block-level cryptographic meta-
data, and ordering-service communications remain based on
classical mechanisms in the evaluated deployment. A cryp-
tographically relevant quantum adversary could therefore
target these infrastructure components even if the stored
ML-DSA-65 signature artifacts remain resistant to quantum
attacks. Accordingly, the proposed scheme constitutes an
incremental application-layer PQC migration step rather than
a complete quantum-safe Hyperledger Fabric architecture.
Achieving broader infrastructure-level quantum resistance
would require a deeper migration of Fabric’s identity, en-
dorsement, communication, ordering, and client-side crypto-
graphic mechanisms.
Complementary confidentiality considerations.The se-
curity scope evaluated in this work concerns application-
layer authenticity and integrity through hybrid ML-DSA-
65/ECDSA signatures, while payload confidentiality repre-
sents a distinct and complementary security objective. For
Fabric applications handling sensitive multimedia content,
content-level encryption could therefore be combined with
the proposed signature architecture to extend protection to
confidentiality. Recent image-encryption approaches based
on a three-dimensional Logistic map [39] and a three-
dimensional memristive cubic map with dual discrete mem-
ristors [40] illustrate potential mechanisms for protecting
image payloads. Related work on video protection includes
segment-selective encryption based on a discrete sinusoidal
memristive Rulkov neuron [41], while a recent review sys-
tematizes chaos-based video-encryption techniques and their
security and performance considerations [42]. These mecha-
nisms address confidentiality rather than signature authentic-
ity and could therefore complement, rather than replace, the
hybrid ML-DSA-65/ECDSA mechanism investigated in this
work. Multimedia encryption is not experimentally evaluated
in the present study and is identified as a potential extension
for Fabric applications requiring confidential image or video
handling.
Multi-instance scalability and availability scope.The
external signing-service architecture supports replication of
the ML-DSA-65 signing component without requiring mod-
ifications to the Fabric network or chaincode interface. As
reported in Section VI-H, a supplementary experiment evalu-
ated two concurrently deployed signing-service instances us-
ing the same persistent ML-DSA-65 key material and deter-
ministic round-robin request distribution. The two-instance
configuration operated consistently at both evaluated submis-
sion rates, while the estimated signing demand remained be-
low 0.3% of the isolated primitive-level capacity per instance.
These results demonstrate that the proposed architecture can
support concurrent multi-instance deployment and request
distribution without changing Fabric’s native transaction-
processing components.
However, the experiment should not be interpreted as
a complete high-availability validation. Automatic failover,
health-aware load balancing, instance-loss recovery, shared-
storage failure, and restart/recovery behavior were not eval-
uated. The present results therefore demonstrate multi-
instance scalability at the signing-service layer, while full
availability and resilience characterization remains a direc-
tion for future work.

level migration.
NIST-standardized algorithms should be preferred.
This work uses ML-DSA-65 as specified in NIST
FIPS 204 [4], rather than pre-standardization Dilithium
variants. Organizations should align their PQC migration
roadmaps with NIST-standardized algorithms to ensure long-
term compliance and interoperability with regulatory require-
ments and industry standards that reference FIPS 204.
E. THREATS TO VALIDITY
The validity of the experimental results is subject to several
threats that must be acknowledged to ensure appropriate
interpretation.
Single-host deployment.All Fabric components were
deployed on a single physical machine communicating over
a Docker bridge network. This eliminates wide-area network
latency, packet loss, and bandwidth constraints that would

be present in a geographically distributed deployment. The
single-host deployment therefore provides a controlled en-
vironment for isolating the relative overhead of the PQC
layer under identical host and container-network conditions.
While the results suggest that the cryptographic signing cost
is unlikely to dominate Fabric latency, they should not be
interpreted as a direct prediction of performance in geograph-
ically distributed production networks.
Synthetic ECDSA baseline delay.The ECDSA baseline
workload injects a synthetic delay of 2.44 ms to equalize the
HTTP round-trip overhead introduced by the PQC microser-
vice. This calibration is based onn= 100measurements
of the microservice latency at unit concurrency and repre-
sents the measured average value. However, microservice
latency varies with system load and concurrency, introducing
a potential source of bias. If the synthetic delay consistently
underestimates or overestimates the true PQC microservice
latency during benchmark runs, the comparison between
configurations may not be perfectly balanced.
Limited topology.The evaluation uses a four-peer, two-
organization topology. Larger networks with more organiza-
tions, more peers per organization, or more complex endorse-
ment policies may exhibit different performance characteris-
tics. In particular, stricter policies involving more organiza-
tions would increase the number of endorsement round-trips
and may alter the relative contribution of the PQC signing
step to end-to-end latency.
Single workload type.The evaluation focuses on a doc-
ument management use case involvingCreateDocument
andSignDocumenttransactions. These transactions rep-
resent a signing-intensive workload in which submitted op-
erations include application-level PQC signature material.
Workloads with different characteristics—such as asset trans-
fer transactions with no application-level signing, or smart
contract logic with complex state interactions—may exhibit
different performance profiles and different sensitivities to
the PQC signature payload.
Sample sizes for secondary scenarios.While the primary
benchmarks usen= 30runs, the stress test and resource
monitoring scenarios usen= 5runs, and the payload
robustness scenarios usen= 9–10runs. These smaller
sample sizes support the absence of observable large effects,
but they offer lower statistical power than the primary sce-
narios. Consequently, small effects may remain undetected
withn= 5. The corresponding results should therefore be
interpreted as supporting evidence rather than as definitive
equivalence tests.
Post-hoc equivalence analysis.The original experimental
protocol was designed around repeated difference testing and
did not prespecify practical equivalence margins before data
collection. Consequently, failure to reject the null hypothesis
in the Welch tests cannot be interpreted as confirmatory
evidence of statistical equivalence. The revised study there-
fore reports Cohen’sdeffect sizes and uses a±10%TOST
margin only as an exploratory sensitivity analysis. Under
this criterion, the primary throughput comparisons satisfy
the exploratory equivalence bounds, whereas the latency
comparisons do not because their 90% confidence intervals
remain wider than the corresponding margins despite neg-
ligible observed effect sizes. A future confirmatory evalua-
tion should define application-relevant equivalence margins
prospectively and determine the required sample size and
statistical power before data collection.

Off-chain ML-DSA-65 verification.The proposed im-
plementation performs ML-DSA-65 cryptographic verifica-
tion off-chain rather than within the chaincode during en-
dorsement. Consequently, the system-level experiments re-
ported in this study do not measure the throughput, la-
tency, or resource-consumption overhead that would result
from chaincode-side ML-DSA-65 verification. The opti-
mizedliboqsimplementation measured an average ML-
DSA-65 verification time of 0.087 ms over 1,000 iterations;
however, this value characterizes only the isolated crypto-
graphic primitive and should not be interpreted as measured
or predicted chaincode-side verification overhead. An on-
chain implementation would additionally involve signature
and public-key decoding, key reconstruction, transaction-
argument processing, chaincode runtime overhead, and con-
current execution by the endorsing peers. Therefore, the per-
formance impact of stronger chaincode-side cryptographic
enforcement remains outside the experimentally validated
scope of this study and should be evaluated through a ded-
icated control experiment in future work.
VIII. CONCLUSION
This paper presented a controlled empirical evaluation of hy-
brid ML-DSA-65/ECDSA signatures in Hyperledger Fabric.
The proposed architecture integrates post-quantum digital
signatures at the application layer through an external ML-
DSA-65 signing microservice, while preserving Fabric’s na-
tive ECDSA-based MSP, endorsement, TLS, and validation
mechanisms. This design provides an incremental migration
path toward post-quantum transaction authentication without
requiring modifications to Fabric core binaries or organiza-
tional identity infrastructure.
The evaluation was conducted on a deployed Hyperledger
Fabric 2.5.13 network composed of two organizations, four
peers, three Raft orderers, CouchDB state databases, and
a Go chaincode deployed using Chaincode-as-a-Service. A
latency-matched ECDSA baseline was compared against the
PQC hybrid configuration across six primary experimental
scenarios covering baseline transaction performance, stress
behavior, payload robustness, and resource consumption,
complemented by cryptographic primitive benchmarking,
block-size analysis, and supplementary targeted experiments.
In addition, a targetedSignDocumentexperiment com-
pared ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87 using
five independent runs per parameter set to examine the effect
of the FIPS 204 security category on signing performance,
Fabric-level throughput and latency, and storage require-
ments.

The results show that ML-DSA-65 signing using the op-
timizedliboqsbackend is computationally lightweight
relative to Fabric transaction latency, with an average signing
time of 0.226 ms. At the transaction level, no statistically sig-
nificant overhead was observed for the primary performance
metrics under the tested workloads. Throughput, average
latency, maximum latency, stress-test behavior, payload-size
robustness, and Fabric infrastructure resource consumption
remained comparable between the ECDSA baseline and the
PQC hybrid configuration. These findings indicate that, un-
der the evaluated conditions, the computational cost of ML-
DSA-65 signing is effectively absorbed by Fabric’s endorse-
ment, ordering, and commit pipeline.
The main practical cost of the proposed hybrid approach
is storage-related. Relative to the functionally equivalent
application-layer ECDSA P-256 baseline, active ML-DSA-
65 blocks are approximately 1.43×larger for signing-
intensiveSignDocumenttransactions.
The proposed approach should be interpreted as an in-
cremental hybrid migration step rather than a complete
quantum-safe Fabric architecture. Fabric’s internal ECDSA
mechanisms, including MSP identities, endorsement signa-
tures, TLS certificates, and ordering-service communica-
tions, remain classical in the evaluated design. Full quantum
resistance would require deeper integration at the Fabric
cryptographic infrastructure level, including BCCSP, MSP,
and TLS layers.
Future work will extend this study in several directions.

and geographically distributed Fabric deployments to mea-

tion, a complete high-availability evaluation remains neces-

partial infrastructure failures. Third, future work should ex-
perimentally evaluate chaincode-side ML-DSA-65 crypto-
graphic verification using a dedicated control configuration.
Such an evaluation should quantify its impact on endorse-
ment latency, end-to-end transaction throughput, chaincode-
container CPU and memory consumption, and behavior un-
der increasing transaction concurrency. This would comple-
ment the primitive-level verification measurement reported
in this study and provide a direct system-level character-
ization of the cost of stronger on-chain cryptographic en-
forcement. Fourth, although the revised evaluation includes
a targetedSignDocumentcomparison of ML-DSA-44,
ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87, future work should extend
ML-DSA-44 and ML-DSA-87 to the complete six-scenario
benchmark suite used for the primary ML-DSA-65 evalua-
tion. This would allow their behavior to be assessed more
comprehensively under stress, payload variation, resource-
consumption, and storage conditions. Alternative standard-
ized post-quantum signature schemes, such as SLH-DSA,
should also be evaluated under the same Fabric workload
model. Finally, storage optimization strategies, including
compact encoding, signature aggregation, off-chain storage
with on-chain commitments, and selective audit trails, should
be explored to reduce ledger growth while preserving post-
quantum auditability.
Overall, the results demonstrate that hybrid ML-DSA-
65/ECDSA signatures can be integrated into Hyperledger
Fabric at the application layer with minimal transaction-
level performance impact under the tested conditions. The
findings support the feasibility of incremental post-quantum
migration for enterprise permissioned blockchain systems,
while highlighting ledger storage overhead as the principal
operational trade-off.

Specification-Driven Synthetic Tabular Data Generation for 
System Validation and Management Decision Support

Abstract. Synthetic tabular data are increasingly needed when real datasets are difficult to 
access, incomplete, or subject to confidentiality constraints, especially when variables must 
comply with prescribed distributions and domain rules. This work proposes and evaluates a 
configurable, specification -driven framework for generating synthetic tabular data that 
respects user-defined distributions and logical exclusion constraints, demonstrated through 
multiple case studies, including IT infrastructure and smart building data. The framework is 
designed to support system validation, benchmarking management systems, and decision -
making under constraints by enabling engineers to fine -tune marginal distributions, enforce 
consistency rules, and scale data generation to millions of rows. It includes a parameter file 
for defining variables, admissible values or intervals, and target percentages, alongside a 
conditions file encoding forbidden combinations as logical rules. The framework 
implements two generation strategies: a sequential baseline and a GPU -accelerated parallel 
method based on CUDA and Numba. Both methods are validated through checks on 
distribution fidelity, constraint satisfaction, null rows, and generation time. Experiments on 
datasets across different domains demonstrate that both methods match target distributions 
with minimal deviations and satisfy all exclusion rules. The parallel implementation

1. Introduction 
Modern IT infrastructures generate large volumes of operational data (Bautista et al., 2019), yet high -
quality datasets for analysis and predictive maintenance remain difficult to obtain. Failures and rare 
events are under -represented, and access to real production logs is often restricted for privacy or 
security reasons. Recorded data may also be incomplete or unbalanced. In this context, synthetic 
tabular data becomes a practical alternative to support model development, stress testing, and 
benchmarking of analytics pipelines for virtualized infrastructures and cloud environments. 
Despite recent advances in generative models for tabular data (Stoian et al., 2025), many 
approaches offer limited control over explicit distributions and domain rules. Practitioners often need 
to enforce precise marginal percentages, numeric intervals, and logical dependencies between 
variables. When these requirements are not met, synthetic datasets can deviate from operational 
constraints, making them hard to trust or reuse. This work addresses the generation of synthetic 
tabular data that accurately reflects user -defined distributions and logical constraints. The framework 
accepts two inputs: a parameter file defining variables, admissible values, and target distributions, and 
a conditions file encoding logical exclusion rules. The resulting synthetic datasets satisfy these 
specifications and support system validation, benchmarking, and decision-making. 
More precisely, the framework aims to: (1) define a general schema and validation workflow for 
parameters and conditions; (2) implement two generation strategies —a sequential baseline and a 
GPU-accelerated parallel method; and (3) evaluate both strategies using a pipeline that checks 
distribution fidelity, constraint satisfaction, null rows, and generation time. This framework is not 
intended to compete with existing generative models such as CTGAN (Xu et al., 2019) or TVAE 
(Kiran et al., 2025), but rather to complement them by providing a fully specification-driven generator 
that enforces explicit distributions and logical constraints defined by the user. 
These capabilities are particularly valuable in regulated or high -stakes environments, where 
operational decisions depend on data that is accurate, reliable, and traceable.

the two generation modes. Section 4 details the IT -infrastructure case study. Section 5 reports and 
discusses the experimental results for both the sequential and parallel implementations. Section 6 
concludes the paper and outlines limitations and future perspectives.

2. Background 
Data generation for advanced applications in IT infrastructure faces numerous challenges that can 
hinder the effectiveness of the models and algorithms. These challenges often stem from issues 
related to data scarcity, dependency complexity, and the limitations of traditional data collection 
methods. 
One of the primary challenges in data generation is the scarcity of high -quality, labeled data. In 
predictive maintenance, particularly for IT infrastructure, obtaining sufficient training data for 
machine learning models is often difficult due to the rarity of failures and anomalies in complex 
systems. These difficulties are further compounded when available data is noisy or imbalanced, 
complicating the training of reliable models (Bansal et al., 2022). 
As predictive maintenance systems increasingly rely on large -scale data from IT and industrial 
infrastructures, data privacy and security have become critical concerns. Traditional centralized 
architectures pose significant risks due to the concentration of sensitive operational data in cloud 
environments, increasing exposure to breaches and non -compliance with regulations such as the 
GDPR (Chen & Zhao, 2012; Zhang, 2018). This is particularly problematic in IT systems, where 
proprietary configurations and sensitive operational metrics are involved.
