II. RELATED WORK
Predictive maintenance (PdM) provides a proactive approach
to anticipate system failures and maintain operational ef-
ficiency. Unlike traditional reactive or preventive mainte-
nance, PdM aims to detect potential issues before they cause
downtime, reducing operational costs and improving overall
system performance. Its effectiveness has been demonstrated
across various domains, including IoT-enabled systems [9],
maritime transport [10], and healthcare systems [11]. By
continuously monitoring system components and analyzing
performance data, PdM enables organizations to schedule
maintenance more effectively and minimize service interrup-
tions.
In IT systems, PdM has been applied using advanced
techniques such as machine learning (ML) and deep learning
(DL). Interpretable ML models have been used to predict
hardware failures in hard drives, providing both accurate
prognostics and explainable insights for system operators
[12]. Deep learning methods, including bidirectional LSTM
networks, have been employed to estimate the remaining
useful life of storage devices and detect early GPU failures
under heavy workloads [13], [14]. AI-powered hardware
failure prediction models have also been proposed to improve
detection accuracy and reduce system downtime [15].
Despite these advances, several challenges remain. Most
models require large amounts of historical data, which may
be incomplete or unavailable for critical components. They
also struggle to handle uncertainty, noise, and missing in-
formation, limiting reliability in real-world IT environments.
Moreover, deep learning models often lack interpretability,
which reduces trust and adoption in critical infrastructures.
Finally, most approaches fail to capture complex causal
interactions among interdependent components, which are
essential for effective maintenance planning.
Recent research addresses these limitations by integrating
probabilistic graphical models with fuzzy logic (FL), provid-
ing transparent and uncertainty-aware decision-making [16].
Fuzzy Bayesian approaches have been applied to predict
disruption risks in warehouse planning [17], manage product
unavailability in inventory systems [18], and assess delivery
delay risks in supply chains [19]. Fuzzy Bayesian Networks
(FBNs) combine quantitative data with expert knowledge,
allowing the modeling of complex causal relationships while
accommodating imprecise or incomplete information.
Applying FBNs to PdM in IT systems represents a novel
direction. This approach models complex causal relation-
ships among critical components, manages uncertain or in-
complete monitoring data, and provides interpretable insights
for proactive maintenance decisions. By combining FL with
Bayesian reasoning, FBNs enable the identification of the
most critical factors influencing component degradation and
overall system reliability, supporting informed maintenance
planning.
Recent work on semi-supervised cross-domain fault di-
agnosis has demonstrated that contrastive pre-training com-
bined with annotation-efficient alignment strategies can sig-
nificantly reduce the need for labeled failure data by lever-
aging unlabeled samples across domains [20]. While such
approaches are powerful when unlabeled operational data is
abundant, our framework targets cold-start scenarios where
even unlabeled failure trajectories are scarce, motivating the
use of expert-elicited fuzzy rules as a substitute for data-
driven feature learning.
In contrast to data-driven predictive maintenance models
(e.g., machine learning on rich failure logs) and classical
reliability or probabilistic risk assessment approaches, the
proposed framework is designed for cold-start scenarios with
scarce failure data, combining fuzzy expert knowledge with
Bayesian network inference to obtain interpretable risk esti-
mates.
III. MODELING THE RISK OF IT SYSTEM FAILURES
USING A FUZZY BA YESIAN NETWORK APPROACH
It is important to note that the proposed framework is vali-
dated as a knowledge-based model rather than a supervised
predictive system. In operational IT environments, fully la-
beled degradation trajectories are rarely available, and critical
failure events are inherently sparse. Consequently, classical
performance metrics such as Precision, Recall, F1-score, or
AUC — which require large labeled failure logs — are not
applicable in this setting. The framework is instead evalu-

The proposed PdM model aims to estimate the risk of
failures in IT systems. To accomplish this objective, the
methodology illustrated in Fig. 1 begins with a comprehen-
sive analysis of critical system components. The first step
involves identifying critical parameters affecting key compo-
nents. An extensive literature review and expert consultations
were conducted to identify failure-related variables and map
their causal relationships. This analysis forms the basis for
constructing a Bayesian Network (BN). Due to the lack
of precise probabilistic data for some events, fuzzy logic
(FL) is integrated to handle uncertainty and imprecision. By
combining fuzzy theory with expert knowledge, rules are
formulated and conditional probabilities are derived.
The resulting Fuzzy Bayesian Network (FBN) integrates
the causal structure of the BN with fuzzy-derived probabili-
ties, allowing assessment of failure probabilities, system state
estimation under various scenarios, and sensitivity analysis.
A. BA YESIAN NETWORK CONSTRUCTION
Bayesian Networks (BNs) are probabilistic graphical models
that provide a principled framework for reasoning under un-
certainty by combining probability theory with graph theory
[22]. Formally, a BN is represented as a directed acyclic
graph (DAG), where each node corresponds to a random
variable and the directed edges denote conditional dependen-
cies between variables [23]. The joint probability distribution
over the network variables is factorized according to the
structure of the DAG:

The quantitative aspect of BNs is defined through con-
ditional probability tables (CPTs) for discrete variables, or
parametric conditional distributions for continuous ones [6].
As shown in Fig. 2, this formalism captures independence
and conditional independence relations between variables,
enabling efficient inference methods such as variable elim-
ination and belief propagation [24].
A key feature of BNs is their ability to dynamically update
beliefs when new evidence becomes available, making them
highly effective for modeling complex systems in fields such
as reliability engineering and predictive maintenance, where
multiple interdependent factors may contribute to system
failures. To assess the risks associated with the failures of IT
systems, a BN was constructed by identifying the relevant
variables and the causal dependencies among them. This
process can be achieved through literature reviews, expert
interviews, brainstorming sessions, or data analysis [25]. Af-
ter constructing the network, an initial validation was carried
out to ensure the reliability and relevance of the model for
PdM. Furthermore, due to the scarcity and imprecision of
historical failure data, conditional probabilities (CPs) were
computed using FL, as detailed in the following section. For
reproducibility, Appendix A provides the detailed step-by-
step algorithm (pseudocode) used to construct the fuzzy–
Bayesian network, including the state definition, fuzzy rule
elicitation, CPT generation, and consistency checks. TA-

are color-coded as follows: input nodes in yellow, interme-
diate nodes in light blue, intermediate nodes with a direct
impact on the final outcome in light green, and the output
node representing overall system reliability in pink.
B. GENERATION OF CONDITIONAL PROBABILITIES
Before generating the fuzzy-based probabilities, it is impor-
tant to distinguish between individual conditional probabil-
ities (CPs) and conditional probability tables (CPTs). A CP
quantifies the likelihood of a specific state of a node given the
states of its parent nodes. These individual probabilities are
grouped into CPTs, which define the complete probabilistic
behavior of each node in the Bayesian Network. Each CPT
reflects all possible combinations of parent states and their
corresponding conditional probabilities.
Assigning CPs to the nodes of the BN is a necessary
step for its effective exploitation. These probabilities can
be determined using two main approaches: objective meth-
ods, which rely on learning algorithms applied to existing
databases, and subjective methods, which draw upon expert
knowledge, often collected through brainstorming sessions.
Since no database specifically covering the parameters of
our BNs exists in the literature, we opted for a subjective
approach.
The study faced the challenge of handling a large number
of conditional probability tables (CPTs), making it imprac-
tical to rely solely on expert knowledge [27]. To overcome
this limitation, a FL approach was adopted. This method
enables the linguistic representation of variable states and the
automatic generation of CPTs, thus reducing the dependence
on repeated expert consultations while improving precision
in modeling [28].

The inference process begins by assigning precise input
values corresponding to the peaks of their Gaussian member-
ship functions, which in turn activate a set of fuzzy rules. A
Sugeno-type fuzzy inference system (FIS) is then employed
to evaluate the degrees of membership for each fuzzy subset.
These calibrated degrees are subsequently used to construct
the CPTs of the BN. In this study, the Sugeno method was
chosen because it avoids the defuzzification step and enables
faster processing, making it suitable for generating the CPTs
required to parameterize the BN [28].
A zero-order Sugeno FIS was used, where each rule con-
sequent is a constant value.
The Zadeh min operator is applied to combine antecedents
(“AND”), and the max operator is used to aggregate the
activation degrees of active rules concluding the same output
label.
Our approach differs from standard Sugeno by using nor-
malized aggregated firing strengths as probability genera-
tors [37], grounded in Zadeh’s possibility theory [34]. This
method interprets activation degrees as relative plausibility
scores and converts them into a sum-one distribution satisfy-
ing Kolmogorov axioms (non-negativity and unit sum).

C. EXPERT P ANEL AND ELICITATION PROCEDURE
The fuzzy rules and conditional probability table (CPT)
entries were elicited from a panel of three experts: a PhD
in computer science and artificial intelligence with around 10
years of industrial experience, a full professor in computer
science with more than 20 years of academic and applied
experience, and a senior engineer with about 8 years of
experience in server-based infrastructures. For each rule and
qualitative state (Normal, Degraded, Critical), experts first
provided their judgements independently. The final label
for each rule was obtained by majority vote; in the rare
cases without majority, a short discussion was used to reach
consensus. Appendix D illustrates this procedure on the
“CPU State” node, showing individual expert decisions and
the resulting final rule set.
During the elicitation sessions, experts were also asked
to rate their confidence in each rule label on a three-level
scale (High, Medium, Low). Rules receiving unanimous
agreement were assigned high confidence; rules resolved by
majority vote or short discussion were assigned medium or
low confidence respectively. This confidence grading directly
informed the magnitude of the Dirichlet perturbation used
in the Monte Carlo uncertainty quantification (Section III-
E): nodes whose CPT rows were elicited with lower expert
consensus were assigned a smaller concentration parameterα
(reflecting wider epistemic uncertainty), while unanimously
agreed rows were assigned a largerα(reflecting tighter
uncertainty). This explicit link ensures that the robustness
analysis reflects not only parametric sensitivity but also the
degree of confidence in the underlying expert judgements.

Evaluation scope and data constraints.The proposed
predictive maintenance approach combines fuzzy logic with
Bayesian inference to explicitly handle uncertainty and in-
complete observations in IT components. In real operational
monitoring logs, fully labeled degradation trajectories are
rarely available and “Critical” events are typically sparse.
As a result, we do not claim a complete supervised eval-
uation across all component states. Instead, we assess the
research quality through (i) structural and probabilistic val-
idation (three-axiom verification and monotonicity tests),
(ii) scenario-based inference analyses, and (iii) robustness
assessment under CPT uncertainty. When labels exist for
observed states, we report quantitative metrics restricted to
those states.
Our evaluation follows a knowledge-based and scenario-
driven protocol (exact Bayesian inference on expert-elicited
CPTs), rather than supervised learning on large i.i.d. labeled
failure logs. Therefore, classical significance tests and sta-
tistical power analysis are not directly applicable to the sce-
nario comparisons because scenarios are not random samples
from a labeled population, and critical events are rare in the
available industrial telemetry. To provide statistical reporting
aligned with this setting, we quantify epistemic uncertainty
in the CPT parameters and report uncertainty intervals on
the key output probabilities. Specifically, we perform Monte

E. SCENARIOS ANTICIP ATION AND INTERPRETATION
After validating the BN model, a set of predictive scenarios
was formulated to estimate the probability of the system
entering a critical state. This was achieved by configuring
the states of the root nodes and analyzing their impacts
through probability propagation. The input variables were
categorized into five groups: CPU-related parameters (user
space, nice, kernel space, hardware interrupts, software in-
terrupts, wait, steal time), RAM-related parameters (active
memory, inactive memory, pages swapped in, fragmenta-
tion rate), GPU-related parameters (GPU usage), hard disk-
related parameters (hard disk usage, UltraDMA CRC error
count, power-on hours), and CSP (ambient temperature, over-
clocking).
Each root variable was assigned one of three op-
erational states based on domain knowledge: Normal
(within nominal limits), Degraded (early-warning lev-
els exceeding thresholds), and Critical (values surpass-
ing failure-risk limits). Expert-guided criteria ensured that
the synthetic scenarios remained realistic, interpretable,
and technically coherent. The resulting six scenarios
are summarized in TABLE 10, and exact root node
state assignments are provided in the supplementary file
root_node_state_assignments.xlsx.
For each scenario, inference was performed through a
deterministic pipeline. All root nodes were fixed using quasi-
certain evidence (probability= 1). The GeNIe Academic

IV . PREDICTIVE MAINTENANCE OF THE SYSTEM
FAILURE USING EVENT TREE ANAL YSIS (ETA)
A. EVENT TREE ANAL YSIS
Event Tree Analysis (ETA) is a probabilistic technique that
models the possible outcomes of a critical initiating event and
the performance of subsequent mitigation measures through
a tree-structured diagram [28]. Within PdM, ETA offers a
structured way to evaluate how preventive and corrective
actions—such as cooling mechanisms, workload balancing,
or administrator intervention—affect the progression of po-
tential failures [47]. By assigning probabilities of success
or failure to each branch, ETA enables the quantification
of system reliability, highlights critical vulnerabilities, and
supports decision-making to reduce downtime and improve
operational resilience.
The development of an event tree generally follows four
steps as illustrated in Fig. 11.
1)Identification of the initiating event:In this study, the
initiating event is the CPU reaching a critical state due
to overheating or overload. This event is not assumed
arbitrarily – its probability is directly derived from the
FBN model presented in Section III. Specifically, when
all CPU input nodes (user space, nice, kernel space,
hardware interrupts, software interrupts, wait, steal
time, ambient temperature, and overclocking) are set
to their critical states, the CPU subnetwork inference
in GeNIe yieldsP(CPU_State=Critical) = 0.984.
This value serves as the initiating event probability
for the ETA, formally chaining the two analyses: the
FBN quantifies the likelihood of the CPU reaching a
critical state, and the ETA evaluates the effectiveness
of subsequent mitigation mechanisms given that this
event has occurred.
2)Definition of intermediate events:Three key mitiga-
tion mechanisms are considered:
•Cooling system activation (success: stabilization
of temperature, failure: persistent overheating).
•Load balancing (success: workload redistribution,
failure: overload maintained).
•Administrator intervention (success: manual re-
covery; failure: unresolved incident).
3)Identification of consequences:Depending on the
success or failure of the intermediate events, the system
may return to a stable operational state or escalate into
a failure state.
4)Quantification of probabilities:The probability of
the final result is calculated by multiplying the prob-
abilities associated with each of the branches [48] that
lead to that outcome, as follows:

highlight the critical importance of cooling efficiency and
administrator intervention in ensuring the reliability of IT
systems.

V . DISCUSSION
The results of the PdM framework demonstrate the critical
influence of component degradation on overall IT system
reliability. Scenario analysis revealed that individual com-
ponent failures, such as hard disk or RAM degradation, can
significantly increase the probability of the system entering a
critical state, while simultaneous failures of multiple compo-
nents almost guarantee system collapse.
Partial sensitivity analysis identified the most influential
parameters at the component level, such as CPU temperature
and load average, RAM fragmentation and overclocking,
GPU usage and VRAM availability, and hard disk error
counts. Global sensitivity analysis further confirmed that
even a single critical component can compromise overall
system stability, emphasizing the importance of proactive
monitoring and maintenance.
The integration of FL into BNs proved effective in han-
dling uncertainty and imprecise expert knowledge, allowing
for interpretable and probabilistically consistent assessment
of failure risks. ETA provided actionable insights into the
effectiveness of different mitigation strategies, highlighting
that cooling systems and timely administrator intervention
are crucial for preserving operational continuity under crit-
ical conditions.
The proposed framework combines a knowledge-based
(rule-based) layer and probabilistic reasoning. Fuzzy IF–
THEN rules encode expert knowledge using linguistic health
states and enable CPT construction under scarce or impre-
cise failure data. Bayesian inference then performs adaptive
belief updating, and maintenance actions are triggered and
scheduled through explicit decision rules, producing an oper-
ational decision-support loop rather than a purely descriptive
reliability assessment.
To illustrate the operational decision-support loop con-
cretely, consider a monitoring cycle in which the BN infer-
ence engine returnsP(System_State=Critical) = 0.85for
a target server. This posterior probability is compared against
a predefined risk thresholdθ= 0.70(configurable by the
operator). Since0.85> θ, the condition check is satisfied.
A persistence filter then verifies whether this threshold has
been exceeded for at least two consecutive monitoring cycles
(e.g., two 5-minute intervals), in order to suppress transient
spikes. If persistence is confirmed, the framework escalates
the alert: a Priority 1 maintenance ticket is automatically
generated, flagging the server for immediate intervention. If
the threshold is exceeded only once (no persistence), a lower-
severity warning (Priority 2) is logged for continued moni-
toring. IfP(System_State=Critical)falls below a second
thresholdθ low = 0.40, no action is triggered and the system
is logged as stable. This rule-based escalation mechanism

critical components and handle uncertainty. The framework

VII. LIMITATIONS, OPERATIONAL CONSIDERATIONS
AND PROSPECTS
A. MODEL LIMITATIONS
The model relies primarily on expert knowledge due to lim-
ited historical failure data. Inaccuracies in expert assessments
and subjective choices in network structure, fuzzy sets, and
membership functions may influence the resulting risk esti-
mates. These limitations highlight the need for progressive
data-driven refinement. In our current industrial context, the
monitored server park generates almost exclusively normal or
mildly degraded states; risk and critical situations are rare and
cannot be induced deliberately. The real dataset we provide
therefore covers only part of the state space and is not suitable
for robust metrics such as AUC, precision/recall or Brier
score. The model should thus be viewed as a knowledge-
based framework for predictive maintenance under data
scarcity rather than a fully validated predictive model learned
from rich failure logs. Note that the Brier-score calibration
reported for CPU State is an internal calibration check on the
elicited probabilities, whereas the real industrial telemetry
does not provide sufficient labeled critical events to compute
robust out-of-sample performance metrics (AUC/precision-
recall/Brier) at the system level.
B. OPERATIONAL DEPLOYMENT CONSIDERATIONS
Telemetry and Data Management:Continuous monitoring
requires sampling rates consistent with system dynamics
and data-retention policies that support real-time diagnos-
tics, incident traceability, and periodic model updates. The
computational requirements of online inference, including
periodic CPT re-evaluation, remain compatible with edge or
on-premise deployment.
Thresholds and Trade-offs:The framework outputs
P(System State=Critical), which must be mapped to main-
tenance actions through a decision thresholdθ. Threshold
selection should reflect organizational cost–benefit consider-
ations by balancing false alarms and missed detections.
Security and Privacy:Telemetry streams may reveal sen-
sitive operational information. Deployment requires appro-
priate protective mechanisms, including encryption, access
control, and data minimization or anonymization.
Model Updates:Static CPTs limit long-term adaptability.
In operational settings, expert-derived parameters should be
periodically refined through Bayesian updating or maximum-
likelihood estimation using newly collected failure data. Per-
formance should be validated on holdout sets before deploy-
ing updated models.
In practice, operators should expect that meaningful data-
driven validation and automatic parameter updating will only
be possible after long-term collection of rare failure and near-
failure events.
C. FIELD TRIAL ROADMAP
A staged deployment supports practical adoption:
1)Pilot phase:Apply the model to representative sys-
tems, collect baseline telemetry, and establish failure
labels.
2)Controlled phase:Enable alerts with human review
and adjust thresholds and CPTs based on observed
errors.
3)Production phase:Conduct progressive rollout while
monitoring detection performance, false-alarm rates,
and advance warning times.
D. FUTURE WORK
Future work includes expanding real-world data collection,
extending the framework to dynamic fuzzy Bayesian net-
works, and enabling automatic optimization of membership
functions and CPT parameters through Bayesian learning
or evolutionary methods. Hybrid approaches that combine
fuzzy Bayesian networks with supervised learning models
may further enhance predictive performance while preserv-
ing interpretability. Expanding real-world data collection,
learning CPTs from observed logs, and comparing the pro-
posed FBN with a classical BN (without fuzzification) and
standard ML baselines (e.g., random forest, survival models)
on shared test sets using standard metrics (AUC, preci-
sion/recall, Brier score, calibration).
E. INDUSTRIAL RELEVANCE AND IMPLEMENTATION
CHALLENGES
The proposed predictive maintenance framework is de-
signed for industrial IT operations where decision-makers
must act under uncertainty, incomplete telemetry, and scarce
labeled failure events. In this setting, a fuzzy Bayesian
network provides interpretable probabilistic outputs (e.g.,
P(System_State=Critical)) that can support maintenance
planning, incident triage, and risk-based prioritization of
interventions. The model is suitable for cold-start contexts
because it can integrate expert knowledge while remaining
updatable as new operational evidence becomes available.

Deploying the approach in production raises practical
challenges. First, telemetry heterogeneity (different hardware
generations, monitoring agents, sampling rates) requires a
stable mapping from raw metrics to discrete states (Nor-
mal/Degraded/Critical), and this mapping may need peri-
odic revision when infrastructure changes. Second, missing
data and noisy sensors can distort evidence; implementa-
tion should include basic quality checks (outlier filtering,
missing-value handling, and confidence flags) before inject-
ing evidence into the BN. Third, expert-elicited probabilities
introduce epistemic uncertainty and potential bias; organiza-
tions should manage this via structured elicitation, periodic

From an engineering perspective, the workflow can be
integrated into existing monitoring stacks as a lightweight
inference service: (i) collectors produce normalized metrics,
(ii) a state-mapping module discretizes evidence, (iii) the BN

dashboards. Future deployments will evaluate performance
across multiple infrastructures and workload regimes, and

A B S T R A C T  
 
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have emerged as a promising solution for machine learning 
and artificial intelligence algorithms constrained by data availability and accessibility. Financial markets, 
alongside healthcare, present significant challen ges due to data privacy and confidentiality concerns. 
GANs enable researchers to generate synthetic financial data that closely mirrors real -world datasets, 
facilitating advancements in market analysis and modeling. Despite their potential, a comprehensive  
evaluation of GAN -based financial data generation remains limited, necessitating a systematic 
assessment of existing methodologies and findings. This paper presents a systematic review of GAN 
architectures applied to financial data generation and market modeling. Our study is distinguished by its 
comprehensive exploration of various GAN variants and their specific applications within different 
facets of financial markets, including stock price prediction, algorithmic trading, portfolio optimization, 
risk m anagement, and fraud detection. Leveraging thirty relevant papers from four major databases 
(IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, Scopus, and arXiv), we synthesize d key findings, identify challenges, 
and highlight limitations in the application of GANs for financial data generation. Our findings reveal 
that while GANs enhance data privacy and accessibility, they also face limitations such as mode collapse, 
instability during training, and regulatory concerns in financial markets. This qualitative review provides 
valuable insights for researchers and stakeholders, offering a foundation for future studies and innovative 
applications of GANs in financial markets.

1. INTRODUCTION 
 
In today’s fast-paced world, technology has significantly 
transformed the way companies analyze the financial 
markets in which they operate. The volatile nature of 
financial markets requires businesses to remain 
constantly updated on market trends to stay competitive. 
However, obtaining high -quality, real financial data 
relevant to market simulations remains a persistent 
challenge. Whether it is to study market trends , manage 
risks, or conduct competitive analysis, access to essential 
financial data is often restricted due to privacy concerns, 
data sharing limitations, or the prohibitive cost of 
acquiring data. 
As in many other domains  such as healthcare (1, 2), 
facing data accessibility issues, deep learning has played 
a crucial role in advancing data generation techniques (3, 
4). One of its most impactful contributions is the 
development of Generative Adversarial Networks 
(GANs). These networks stem from foundational deep 
learning architectures, particularly those designed for 
unsupervised learning, enabling machines to generate 
highly realistic synthetic data. GANs, first introduced by 
Goodfellow et al. (5), have emerged as a promising 
solution for generating synthetic  financial data. GANs 
can produce artificial datasets that closely replicate the 
statistical distributions and properties of real -world 
financial data. These synthetic datasets not only preserve 
privacy and sensitive information but also provide a 
viable alternative  for stakeholders such as researchers, 
companies, and policymakers. GANs' ability to generate 
high-fidelity financial data has opened new opportunities 
for predictive modeling, financ ial risk assessment, and 
market scenario simulations. 
Since their introduction, numerous variants of GANs 
have been developed, each designed to address specific 
data generation challenges such as images generation (6–
11), audio synthesis  (12) , and tabular data generation  
(13,14), across different domains. Despite these 
advancements, a clear research gap remains in the 
application of GANs for financial data generation. While 
GANs have shown promise in generating realistic 
financial data, challenges persist in areas such as model 
stability, mode collapse, and ensuring that synthetic data 
maintains financial market dynamics while being useful 
for real -world applications. Additionally, few studies 
provide comprehensive evaluations comparing different 
GAN variants on financial datasets, making it difficult to 
determine best practices in this domain. 
To address these gaps, this article presents a 
systematic review of the application of GANs for 
financial data generation, analyzing key scientific 
research  papers  published  between  2019  and  2024. 
Our   study   follows   a   structured   methodology   to  
ensure comprehensive coverage of relevant work. 
Specifically, we: 
- Collect research papers from four major 
academic databases. 
- Define clear inclusion and exclusion criteria for 
selecting relevant studies. 
- Analyze and compare different GAN 
architectures tailored for financial applications. 
- Identify key findings, challenges, and future 
research directions in the field. 
By structuring our review in this manner, we aim ed 
to provide a well -rounded perspective on how GANs 
contribute to financial data generation, highlight the most 
effective architectures, and discuss remaining challenges 
for future research.

3. LITERATURE REVIEW: OVERVIEW OF GAN 
VARIANTS 
 
The concept of Generative Adversarial Networks 
(GANs) was first introduced by Goodfellow and his team 
(5, 25)  in their seminal article "Generative Adversarial 
Networks". In this article, they presented an adversarial 
framework involving two models trained simultaneously 
in competition with each other: a generative model that 
learns and captures the real data dist ribution, and a 
discriminative model that estimates the probability of a 
sample being from the real training data versus the 
generative model.  
The framework requires a considerable amount of 
real dataset as input for training. The primary objective is 
to produce a large set of synthetic data that closely 
resembles the real data distribution. During the training 
phase, the generative model aims to  maximize the 
likelihood of the discriminative model making a mistake, 
while the discriminative model works to maximize its 
ability to distinguish between real and fake data 
generated by the generative model. This adversarial 
process can be illustraed in Figure 2 (26).  
This foundational concept has since inspired the 
development of numerous GAN variants, each designed 
to address specific challenges or cater to particular 
applications. Table 1 summarized our systematic review, 
we present a comprehensive analysis of 16 cas es as the 
most important GAN variants among those currently 
available. For each variant, we highlight its primary 
purpose and key characteristics, providing an in -depth 
overview of their unique contributions and applications.

5. CHALLENGES AND OPEN RESEARCH 
DIRECTIONS 
 
Although Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) 
were first introduced in 2014, their application to 
financial data generation and market modeling only 
gained traction around 2019. In this systematic review we 
have highlighted how  GANs have been employed in 
various aspects of financial markets, such as portfolio 
analysis, stock price prediction, and market simulation. 
However, several challenges and limitations remain in 
generating financial data using GANs. In this section we 
outline key challenges and pote ntial future research 
directions.   
5. 1. Challenges In Applying GANs To Financial 
Data: Data Limitations and Quality Issues            
While financial markets generate vast amounts of data, 
high-quality, clean, and sufficiently granular datasets 
remain scarce. GANs require extensive training data, and 
noisy or incomplete datasets can significantly impact 
their performance. Additionally, financial datasets often 
suffer from structural breaks, non -stationarity, and 
regulatory-driven changes, making it difficult to maintain 
consistent data quality over time.

Limited stability in training GANs:  Many articles

to the adversarial nature of GANs, making it challenging 
to achieve consistent results, particularly when dealing 
with volatile market data.  Furthermore, mode collapse 
remains a persistent problem, where the generator 
produces a limited set of repetitive outputs instead of 
capturing the full distribution of financial patterns. To 
mitigate this, techniques such as Wasserstein GANs 
(WGANs) (27), gradient penalty regularization, and 
improved loss functions need to be explored further. 
Model evaluation and benchmarking:  At the time 
of this systematic review, there is no universally accepted 
evaluation metric for assessing GAN-generated financial 
data. The variants of GANs covered in this study rely on 
distributional metrics or dependence measures, but a 
unified approach that incorporates financial risk, market 
efficiency, and predictive performance is still lacking. 
Capturing market dynamics and competitive 
aspects: While those GANs have been effective in 
modeling asset prices and volatility, they rarely account 
for competitive market dynamics such as interactions 
between market participants, market microstructure, and 
strategic competition. Incorporating these elements 
remains an open challenge. 
Model training complexity and stability: Advanced 
models such as transformer-based GANs (e.g., TTGAN) 
require extensive computational resources, 
hyperparameter tuning, and large datasets. Training 
instabilities, such as mode collapse, make it challenging 
to generate diverse market scenarios. Moreover, 
overfitting can occur when GANs memorize specific 
patterns in historical financial data rather than learning 
generalizable features, particularly in small or highly 
correlated datasets. Regularization techniqu es and 
differential privacy methods could be useful to address 
this issue. 
Long-range dependencies and market regimes:  
Financial markets are highly non -linear and subject to 
sudden regime shifts (e.g., market crashes, economic 
policy changes). While attention-based GANs (TAGAN, 
TTGAN) improve the modeling of long -range 
dependencies, they still struggle with capturing regi me 
changes and extreme market events.  One potential 
approach to addressing this limitation is integrating 
GANs with regime -switching models, such as Hidden 
Markov Models (HMMs) or recurrent neural networks 
(RNNs) with state transitions, to detect and adapt to 
sudden shifts in market. Additionally, developing hybrid 
models that incorporate time -varying risk factors and 
sentiment analysis could enhance the adaptability of 
GANs to real-world financial conditions. 
Economic aspect of the market in general:  Most 
studies focus on applying GANs to financial markets, 
such as asset price modeling, stock market prediction, 
and risk management. However, broader macroeconomic 
dynamics remain largely unexplored. There is a lack of 
research using GANs to model global economic 
phenomena such as, inflation, business cycles, and the 
impact of monetary and fiscal policies. Expanding GAN 
applications to these areas could provide valuable 
insights into complex economic systems and po licy-
making. 
 
5. 2. Open Research Directions :  Incorporating 
Market Competition and Strategic Interactions           
Future research can explore GANs that model 
competitive market environments with multiple agents 
employing diverse trading strategies. Game -theoretic 
could be used to simulate strategic interactions in trading, 
regulatory impacts, and competitive behaviors. 
Improving Tail Modeling and Extreme Event 
Simulation: Financial markets exhibit heavy tails and 
extreme events, yet existing GAN models often fail to 
capture these accurately. While some studies use the 
Lambert W transformation to address heavy tails, further 
improvements are needed to enhance GANs' ability to 
simulate rare financial events such as market crashes.  A 
promising direction would be the development of GAN 
architectures incorporating extreme value theory (EVT) 
or tail-risk-aware loss functions to better model financial 
anomalies. 
Integration with Real -Time Data for Continuous 
Market Analysis: Developing GAN models that can be 
continuously updated with incoming market data could 
enable real -time market monitoring and adaptive 
strategies. This could involve using streaming GANs or 
online learning techniques, allowing models to evolve 
with changing market conditions while avoiding 
overfitting to outdated patterns. 
Combining GANs with Reinforcement Learning 
for Market Simulation:  Hybrid models that integrate 
GANs with reinforcement learning could enable dynamic 
market simulations where agents adapt their strategies 
over time, leading to more realistic and robust market 
models.

6. CONCLUSION 
 
This systematic review has explored the application of 
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in the 
generation of financial data and market modeling. Our 
qualitative analysis was based on 30 relevant research 
papers published across four databases: Web of  Science, 
Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and ArXiv. To the best of our 
knowledge, this review is the first to explore not only the 
various GAN models since their inception in 2014 but 
also to highlight their application specifically within 
financial markets.  
Our analysis highlights key market aspects addressed 
by GAN applications, including portfolio analysis, risk 
management, market simulation, and stock market 
analysis (see Table 2). Our findings highlight that while

GANs have demonstrated strong capabilities in 
generating high -fidelity financial data, certain market 
aspects, such as market competition, strategic 
interactions, long -range dependencies, and market 
regimes remain underexplored. Furthermore, we 
identified key challenges in applying GANs to financial 
data generation, including issues related to mode 
collapse, data biases, and evaluation metrics. Future 
research could integrate GANs with Reinforcement 
Learning for market simulation and develop GAN 
models that better address competitive market dynamics.  
Despite the robust findings of this review, the 
keywords used for data collection may have influenced 
the scope of the selected studies. Hence, future research 
could benefit from employing alternative keyword 
strategies to enrich the breadth of analyzed literature.

ABSTRACT Detecting anomalies in the injection molding process remains a challenging task, demanding
significant resources, data, and expertise due to their impact on cost and time reduction. While traditional
methods like statistical process control (SPC) using control charts are widely used for detecting irregularities,
they can catch predefined patterns such as systematic, upward shift, downward shift, cyclic, and mixture
patterns. However, they still have limitations in identifying anomalies beyond theses common patterns.
Numerous unnatural patterns may exist in process data, indicating that the process is out of control. In our
study, we propose an innovative strategy to enhance anomaly detection by integrating Statistical Process
Control (SPC) with a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) based Autoencoder (AE). The main objective is
to detect variations in the Melt cushion parameter, a crucial aspect of the injection molding process. The
LSTM-AE model determines optimal threshold levels based on reconstruction loss rates across all time-
series sequences, complementing traditional control charts’ upper and lower limits. With a model achieving a
coefficient of determination (R-squared) of 0.993 and a Mean Absolute Error of 0.0146 through training, and
incorporating multiple process limits—Upper Limit Control (ULC), Lower Limit Control (LLC), Maximum
Threshold, and Minimum Threshold—the enhanced control chart exhibits significant advancements in
anomaly detection. In four distinct scenarios, the integrated model demonstrates its capability to detect
anomalies in the Melt cushion that exceed predefined limits, as well as anomalies showing ascending and
descending trends. This ultimately enhances the robustness and efficiency of anomaly detection in injection
molding processes.
INDEX TERMS Injection molding process, melt cushion parameter, anomaly detection, statistical process
control, LSTM-auto encoder.

By identifying and addressing potential equipment failures
before they occur, manufacturers can minimize downtime,

The need to identify anomalies in industrial processes,
especially in injection molding, has driven extensive research
into various statistical methodologies. These methods aim
to pinpoint deviations from normal operating conditions,
enabling timely interventions and process optimization.
Among the tools used for anomaly detection, the main
methodologies include Moving Average, Cumulative Sum,
Deep Learning with Probability, and Statistical Process
Control (SPC) [5].
As shown by Cox [6], The Moving Average is foundational
statistical technique that calculates the average of a sliding
window of data points, enabling the detection of shifts or
trends in process behavior over time. On the other hand,
Cumulative Sum, as demonstrated by Grunkemeier et al. [7],
allows tracking the cumulative deviation from a specified
reference value, facilitating the early detection of persistent
process shifts or abnormalities. Additionally, Deep Learning
with Probability, as demonstrated by Ketonen and Blech [8],
leverages advanced neural network architectures. Deep
learning techniques combined with probabilistic models offer
enhanced capabilities for anomaly detection, particularly in
complex and high-dimensional datasets. Among the most
widely utilized tools within the Statistical Process Control
framework are the control charts. These charts, including the
X-bar and R (Range) charts for monitoring process mean and
deviation, provide a systematic approach to tracking process
stability and detecting deviations from established control
limits [9]. Integrating these statistical approaches not only
enables the identification of anomalies, but also empowers
manufacturers to proactively manage process variability,
optimize production efficiency, and uphold product quality
standards. Several studies have explored the application of
the control charts in injection molding processes. Rohani
and Chan [10] employed quality tools and control charts
to enhance the quality of plastic injection molded lenses
utilized in telecommunication devices. Their study showed
the ability to decrease the defect rate from 13.49% to 10%.
Chaciński et al. [11] deployed Statistical Process Control,
integrating process capability indicators and performance
indicators into their study. They assessed three product
types, focusing on product mass to improve defect detection,
meet customer specifications, and reduce non-compliance.
Cao et al. [12] introduced an approach using SPC principles.
They utilized data from different parts to create control
charts tailored to specific part families. The objective of
their method is to streamline the intricate injection molding
process, facilitating swift identification and response to
defects while enhancing the efficiency of the control system
as a whole.
From the literature review, statistical process control
remains one of the most widely used methods for anomaly
detection. However, despite the benefits it offers, Statistical
Process Control (SPC) also comes with limitations, which can
be summarized into four main points:
• Limitations in complex processes: SPC is most effective
in processes with stable and predictable behavior.
In highly complex processes with numerous interacting
variables, it can be challenging to isolate the effects of
individual factors and identify root causes of variation.
This complexity may result in overlooking critical
factors or interactions, leading to incomplete insights
into process behavior.
• Assumption of normal distribution [13]: SPC techniques
such as control charts often assume that process
data follows a normal distribution. However, in real-
world scenarios, process data may exhibit non-normal
distributions due to various factors such as asymmetry
or multimodality. When data deviates significantly
from normality, the effectiveness of SPC methods
may be compromised, potentially leading to inaccurate
conclusions or decisions.
• Overreliance on historical data: SPC relies heavily
on historical data to establish control limits, identify
patterns, and make process adjustments. While historical
data provides valuable insights into past performance,
it may not always capture future changes or variations
in the process. Unforeseen events, process improve-
ments, or changes in operating conditions may not
be adequately accounted for in historical data, leading
to suboptimal decisions or actions based on outdated
information.
• Delayed detection of changes: SPC is designed to
detect significant shifts or trends in process behavior
over time. However, it may not always promptly
detect small or rapid changes that occur within short
timeframes. These small changes, if left undetected,
can accumulate over time and impact product quality
or process performance. Additionally, SPC methods
may have limitations in detecting changes in certain
types of variation, such as sporadic or systematic
shifts, leading to delayed responses and potential quality
issues.

II. SCOPE OF STUDY
A. INJECTION MOLDING PROCESS
Injection molding, a widely used plastic manufacturing
process, comprises five key steps: Plasticizing, injection,
packing, cooling, and ejection [17]. During plasticizing,
plastic material is fed into a heated cylinder via a hopper and
processed by a rotating screw. Friction and heating units melt
the material, accumulating it at the screw tip until pressure
prompts the screw to retract, creating a melt reservoir. The
injection phase starts when the mold closes, and the molten
material fills it. Following this, packing, cooling, and ejection
occur. Once solidified, the part is ejected as the mold opens,
completing the cycle [18]. This process is facilitated by an
injection molding machine.
Figure 1 illustrates the principal components of the injec-
tion equipment. The injection machine is a complex system
with several essential components, including the injection
system and mold clamping mechanism. The injection system
comprises the hopper, where raw material is stored, the
barrel where it’s melted and homogenized, the screw system
for injecting material into the mold, and the nozzle for the
injection point [19]. Conversely, the clamping unit consists
of the mold, which shapes the final product, the clamping
mechanism that securely holds the mold halves together
during injection, and the ejector mechanism, which opens
the mold and ejects the finished part once it’s cooled and
solidified.

III. LITERATURE REVIEW
Many research has been explored into anomaly detection
aspects, this review focuses on three main areas of anomaly
detection: injection molding processes, Statistical Process
Control (SPC) in injection molding, and Long Short-Term
Memory Autoencoder (LSTM-AE) techniques for general
anomaly detection.
At the level of anomaly detection, several approaches
have been explored. Lughofer and Pichler [23] propose an
automated method for predicting quality issues in injection
molding machines using only regular production data. Their
approach analyzes process variables to detect anomalies and
predicts quality criteria directly from time series trends.
By dynamically updating models, they successfully identified
anomalies and production changes during real processes,
achieving high correlations up to 0.98, with observed quality
trends and low error rates below 5%. Lee et al. [24] explore
the growing significance of smart factories, particularly in
sensor data-based anomaly detection research. They present
a framework that utilizes sensor data obtained from plastic
injection machines along with deep learning models to detect
anomalies and securely cluster outliers. This framework aims
to provide effective solution tailored for factories transition-
ing to smart factory systems, with three main contributions.
Firstly, it adopts a suitable approach for manufacturing sites.
Secondly, it secures outliers using Auto Label with pseudo
labeling. Thirdly, it enables decision-makers to identify
potential defect causes. The benefits of this approach are
incorporated into the Two Phases Anomaly Detection system
architecture, which utilizes an LSTM classifier alongside
the pseudo labeling technique, achieving a high reliability
rate surpassing 90% accuracy. Additionally, clustering visu-
alization of defective data is facilitated through the Self
Organizing Map (SOM) algorithm. Nunes et al.[25] highlight
the importance of predictive maintenance in industry for
optimizing maintenance schedules and prolonging equipment
lifespan. They introduce a data-driven methodology called
generalized fault trees to assess equipment reliability in real-
time. Applied to predictive maintenance of injection molds,
their approach, combining a new training algorithm with
isolation forest anomaly detection, demonstrates significant
cost savings of 27.05% compared to preventive mainte-
nance and 63.43% compared to corrective maintenance.
Silva et al. [26] discuss the implementation of Artificial
Intelligence (AI) in plastic injection molding processes to
enhance competitiveness in Industry 4.0. They highlight the
importance of real-time Quality Prediction methodologies in
reducing costs for companies dealing with complex industrial
processes. The paper delineates the implementation process,
encompassing data collection, real-time classification, and
methodologies such as Data Augmentation and Human-
in-the-Loop labeling. The AI-driven approach enables pre-
diction and alerting of process quality issues, leading to
increased productivity and reduced non-compliant parts
production. Testing across various processes and materials
shows significant improvements, including up to a 12%

C. SPC FRAMEWORK
1) PROCESS CAPABILITY
As defined by Oberoi et al. [40], Process capability is
a statistical metric that gauges the capacity of a process
to consistently generate output that aligns with predefined
criteria or customer expectations. In other words, it assesses
the extent to which a process can meet quality standards
within the tolerance limits set for the product. The capability
of a process is typically evaluated in terms of its ability
to perform within specified upper and lower limits or
tolerances. These tolerances represent the acceptable range of
variation for key characteristics or dimensions of the product
or service. Process capability analysis aims to determine
whether the inherent variability of the process is small
enough to ensure that the majority of output falls within
these tolerance limits. The most commonly used indices for
evaluating process capability are Cp and Cpk
• Cp (Process Capability Index): Process capability
assesses a process’s ability to meet specifications by
evaluating the spread of the process distribution relative
to the width of the specification limits. It’s calculated as
the ratio of the tolerance width to the process variation,
expressed by the following formula:
Cp = (USL - LSL)/6σ (1)
where USL is the upper specification limit, LSL is the lower
specification limit and σ is the standard deviation of the
process.
• Cpk (Process Capability Index, adjusted for centering):
Is similar to Cp but also takes into account the centering
FIGURE 7. Analysis of capability using the provided normal dataset.
of the process relative to the target or nominal value.
It evaluates both the spread of the process distribution
and its alignment with the target value. Cpk is calculated
as the minimum of two indices, the minimum distance
between the process mean and the nearest specification
limit, expressed as follows:
Cpk = min((USL − µ)/3σ, (µ − LSL)/3σ )) (2)
where µ is the mean of the values, USL represents the upper
specification limit, LSL stands for the lower specification
limit, and σ denotes the standard deviation of the process.
Cp assesses if the distribution can fit within the specifi-
cation limits, while Cpk determines if the overall average
is centered. When the overall average aligns with the
specification center, Cp and Cpk values match. If they differ,
it indicates the overall average is not centered. The greater the
gap between the values, the more the overall average is offset.
Palmer and Tsui [42] explained that the interpretation of
the process can be done according to the value obtained of
each capability index:
• If (Cp > 1 and Cpk > 1): The process is capable, and the
process mean is well-centered within the specification
limits. This is the ideal scenario, and it signifies that the
process has a low probability of producing defects.
• If (Cp > 1 and Cpk < 1): The process is capable, but
the process mean is not well-centered. This suggests that
although the process can produce within specifications,
there is a risk of producing a higher proportion of defects
due to the lack of centering.
• If (Cp < 1 and Cpk < 1): The process is not capable,
and the process mean is not well-centered. This indicates
that the process is producing a substantial number of
defects, and immediate actions are required to improve
the process

2) THEORY OF CONTROL CHART
Control charts are essential tools in statistical process control
(SPC) for monitoring and controlling processes in real time
[43]. Figure 8 shows visual representation of typical control
chart. The selection of a control chart type depends on the
characteristics of the data being monitored and the specific
goals of the analysis [44].
Figure 9 illustrates the common types of control charts,
which are classified into two main types: attributes, as dis-
cussed by Chiu and Kuo [45], and variables, as elaborated
by Gibra [46]. Attribute control can be subdivided into charts
for percentage defectives and charts for the number of defects
per unit. In variables control, the main emphasis is placed
on monitoring fluctuations in the average and the range
of measurements. Regardless of the specific type, control
charts generally adhere to the same fundamental structure,
where the mean value is enclosed by upper and lower
control limits. The calculation of these control limits varies
depending on the type of chart being used. In this paper, based
on the measurable value and sample size, we utilized the
X-Bar and Range control chart concept to define the Upper
Limit Control (ULC) and Lower Limit Control (LCL) of the
process. This approach was also used to generate the new
dataset for the LSTM-Auto encoder, with samples consisting
of 3 observations each.

2) AUTOENCODER
Autoencoder is unsupervised learning technique used to
build data-driven models when labeled data is unavailable.
The learning process of the Autoencoder model involves
predicting input data and minimizing the difference, known
as the reconstruction loss (RL), from the input to the output.
Figure 13 illustrates the architecture of the proposed AE,

the decoder [52]. The decoder layer is composed of two
LSTM layers, one with 32 units and the other with 64 units.
Subsequently, the decoder’s output is transformed into a
time series distribution that reflects the characteristics of
the input data. The LSTM-AE model acquires knowledge
from the training dataset by reducing the loss associated with
reconstruction with both input data (xt) and output data (yt).

mean absolute error (MAE), as in (18).

b: LSTM ENCODER
The primary function of the LSTM encoder is to serve as a
sequence folding layer, transforming features into a batch of
feature sequences organized by time. This process resembles
applying convolution operations separately to each timestep
of the feature sequences. Figure 14 illustrates how the AE
encoder collaborates with a sequence of LSTM unit cells,
which have been trained to discern the crucial features within
the input sequence.
Each time series of Xi comprises 5 samples gathered over
5 timesteps. This data is then inputted into the encoder.
The first layer receives as input sequences with dimension
according to the features and timesteps, on our case the
feature is 1 and the timesteps is 5, the input is [5 × 1], the
process is obtained on parallel mechanism between each cells
and each timesteps of the sequences, the output of this layer
is sequence with dimensional of [5 ∗64]. The second layer
consists of an LSTM network containing 32 LSTM cells.
Each LSTM cell unit is responsible for processing a single
sample. A sequence of 5 LSTM cells operates sequentially,
where the first LSTM unit transfers the outcome of the sample
to the second LSTM unit. Following this, the second LSTM
unit evaluates whether to preserve or discard the preceding
sample from the first LSTM. If it opts to preserve it, the
information is stored in long-term memory. Then, the second
LSTM cell transmits the information of the sample from the
first LSTM cell, along with the feature information processed
from the current sample, to the third LSTM cell, and so on.
The final LSTM cell, which is the fifth in the sequence,
integrates all the samples considered valuable, as processed
by the preceding four LSTM cells. The final LSTM cell
outputs the information pertaining to all relevant samples.

V. DISCUSSION
The current paper introduces a fusion of the Statistical
Process Mean Control Chart with LSTM Autoencoder
to improve the detection of anomalies in the injection
molding process, focusing specifically on the ‘‘Melt Injection
Parameter’’ as a case study. The key findings of this study can
be outlined as follows:
• Smart control charts: The control chart of the mean
are enhanced by introducing two additional limits,
the minimum and maximum thresholds, alongside the
existing lower and upper control limits (LLC and
ULC). This paper affirms that such augmentation sig-
nificantly boosts anomaly detection capability. Unlike
the static LLC and ULC, the min and max limits are
dynamic, allowing for adjustments based on application
requirements and the severity of anomaly detection.
The determination of these limits often relies on expert
analysis. Through experimentation with different min
and max limit values, the type of anomalies detected can
vary. In our study, four types were identified. The initial
trial, utilizing 0.0277 as the maximum and 0.0277 as
the minimum, only detected one type of anomaly, while
trial 4, with 0.243 as the maximum and 0.0188 as the
minimum, identified all four types.

predefined limits but also discerns the ascending and

of anomalies is crucial for initiating timely actions
to prevent process deviations and make adjustments
before defective parts are produced or any machine
malfunctions occur.
This study presents two main limitations that can be
addressed separately to further enhance the quality of the
results.
• Firstly, the quantity of data is crucial for deep learning
models to achieve high performance in detecting a
diverse range of anomalies and making accurate pre-
dictions. In this paper, the trained model was based
on data initially derived from 10160 values, which
were divided into three samples according to the mean
control chart, yielding 3389 values. Since the model
heavily relies on error reconstruction, having more data
would improve precision in error reconstruction and
subsequently enhance detectability.
• Secondly, a limitation lies in the model’s dependency on
training with normal situations. Ideally, achieving such
normal conditions is complex in real-world scenarios
due to the degradation and life cycle of machines. Condi-
tions such as machine state, materials used, maintenance
protocols, and labor factors all need to align optimally,
which can be challenging to replicate simultaneously
in experimental settings. Addressing these limitations
could lead to more robust and applicable results in
anomaly detection and prediction.
• Finally, the real-world conditions frequently involve
complex interactions among variables that evolve over

norms. By incorporating these supplementary sensors into
our data collection framework, future research efforts can aim
to achieve a more comprehensive understanding of equipment
behavior and performance. This enhanced visibility can
facilitate more proactive anomaly detection and mitigation
strategies, ultimately contributing to improved manufacturing
efficiency and product quality.
VI. CONCLUSION
The present paper introduces a novel approach that combines
Statistical Process Control (SPC) with LSTM-Autoencoder
(LSTM-AE) to enhance anomaly detection in injection
molding processes, focusing on the critical parameter of
‘‘Melt Injection.’’ The study demonstrates the efficacy of
this hybrid methodology in detecting anomalies, including
early detection and trend analysis of deviations in the
manufacturing process. Moreover, the research highlights
the importance of integrating advanced machine learning
techniques with traditional process control methods to
improve quality assurance and prevent defects in industrial
settings. By leveraging the strengths of both SPC and LSTM-
AE, the proposed approach offers a promising solution
for real-time monitoring and proactive management of
production processes.
Overall, this study contributes valuable insights to the
field of anomaly detection in manufacturing, paving the
way for further advancements in process optimization and
quality control. The findings underscore the potential of
hybrid methodologies to enhance efficiency, reduce costs,
and ensure product quality in industrial operations.

 Support ticket system (STS) is one of the most critical 
customer relationship management (CRM) solutions 
through which companies are capable  of manag ing 
customer requests properly [1] [2]. 
This paper presents a comparison of the performance of 
three methods to predict ticket recurrence with Support 
Vector Machines (SVM), which is a suitable algorithm for 
binary classification. The first method uses Jaccard 
similarity; the second uses Cosine similarity and the 
third uses SBERT and Cosine s imilarity by a hybrid 
approach [3] [4] [5]. 
The comparison of the three techniques regarding the 
performance of prediction based on accuracy indicates 
that the Jaccard -based approach is 0.7419 accurate, 
whereas applying Cosine Similarity provides much 
better performance at 0.8710. The hybrid procedure of 
SBERT and Cosine Similarity yields the best possible 
accuracy at 0.9355 and identifies that the hybrid 
procedure significantly boosts the predictive potential of 
the model in predicting ticket recurrence.

A B S T R A C T  
 
 
In injection molding manufacturing, selection of the optimal machine from various alternatives is a 
crucial strategy for enhancing productivity, cost-effectiveness, and maintaining performance standards. 
This article presents an approach that combines two techniques to make the best choice from three 
presented options. Firstly, it employs the Analytic Hierarchy Process method to deter mine the weights 
of five main criteria and eleven sub-criteria, considering both cost and performance. Secondly, it utilizes 
the Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution to rank the three machines by 
comparing each machine's performance against ideal and anti-ideal solutions to determine their relative 
suitability. The final model is validated through three distinct scenarios, illustrating how key criteria such 
as cost breakdown and scrap rate can influence the ultimate selection ranki ng. Through a presented 
numerical example, the paper provides decision -makers with a scientifically robust decision support 
system, aiding in strategic and complex decision -making processes for selecting the most suitable 
machine.

1. INTRODUCTION 
 
The injection molding process is widely known as a one 
of the most used technique adopted by the plastic 
manufacturing industry, renowned for its ability to 
produce high -quality and precise components at a 
moderate cost (1, 2). Polymer products find application 
in a wide array of industries, including automotive  (3), 
aerospace, and civil engineering (4). 
In the context of the profitability optimization inside 
the production workshop, selection the optimum machine 
from several alternatives still one of the challenging task 
in the field of injection molding manufacturing, which is 
recognized as a multi-criteria decision-making challenge, 
usually managed by professionals and experienced 
adjusters (5).  
The paper explore two main challenges encountered 
in real workshop settings: 
 Traditional methods involve selecting a machine 
based on technical characteristics such as clamping 
force, distance between tie bars, and maximum 
volume of shotting. However, a single product may 
be suitable for multiple machines. To address this, 
the ques tion arises: if a product is technically 
validated for production on three different

 Traditional methods involve selecting a machine 
based on technical characteristics such as clamping 
force, distance between tie bars, and maximum 
volume of shotting. However, a single product may 
be suitable for multiple machines. To address this, 
the ques tion arises: if a product is technically 
validated for production on three different 
alternatives, which one is the optimal choice based 
on production performance and historical data? This 
challenge prompts the need to determine the best 
machines based on both performance and production 
cost, thereby completing the technical decision -
making process. 
 How can we employ a scientific and technical 
approach from various existing methods to make the 
optimal choice? This challenge highlights the 
necessity of utilizing a systematic approach to select 
the best option among multiple existing approaches, 
ensuring the most effective decision -making 
process. 
In this context, addressing the selection problem 
involves navigating through a multiple of criteria and 
sub-criteria while considering conflicting objectives such 
as performance and production costs. This article 
addresses the selection problem associated with injection 
molding machines using multi -criteria decision -making 
(MCDM) framework  (5, 6). The main principle of the 
suggested approach is based on combination of two 
models, the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) (7) and 
Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal 
Solution (TOPSIS) (8, 9) methodologies to facilitate 
decision-making in injection molding machine selection. 
By integrating AHP and TOPSIS, present study aims to 
present decision -makers with a comprehensive and 
structured approach to tackle the complexity of injection 
molding machine selection. The proposed methodology 
enables the prioritization of alternative machines based 
on their performance acro ss multiple criteria, thereby 
facilitating informed decision -making and enhancing 
overall manufacturing efficiency. Through the 
application of the proposed approach, manufacturers can 
achieve better alignment between machine capabilities 
and production requirements, leading to improve quality, 
enhanced productivity, and optimized production costs in 
injection molding operations. Five main criteria are 
identified for evaluation, namely quality, machine 
availability, performance, operating cost, and investment 
cost. The five criteria com prise nine sub -criteria, 
including rework rate, scrap rate, breakdown rate, 
changeover time, production speed, micro stoppage 
frequency, energy consumption, labor cost, maintenance 
cost, purchasing price, and installation cost. 
The article provides specific contributions which can 
be summarized as follows: 
 Framework Development: The article introduces a 
structured framework tailored for managers and 
technical experts engaged in the injection molding 
sector. This framework provides a systematic 
approach to decision-making, guiding users through 
the process of selecting the most suitab le options 
based on predetermined criteria 
 Case Study Illustration: Presenting case studies with 
real data extracted from automotive workshops, 
demonstrating the practical application of the 
proposed method. 
 Weighting Criteria with  AHP: The article employs 
the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) method to 
assign appropriate weights to eleven of criteria used 
in the decision-making process. AHP allows for the 
prioritization of criteria based on their relative 
importance, ensuring that c ritical factors receive 
adequate consideration in the decision -making 
process. 
 Optimal Choice with TOPSIS: Following the 
determination of criteria weights using AHP, the 
article applies the Technique for Order Preference by 
Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) method. This 
involves ranking the available options based on their 
similarity to the ideal solution and their distance 
from the negative ideal solution. Notably, the AHP 
results serve as inputs to the TOPSIS analysis, 
enhancing the precision and effectiveness of the 
decision-making process. 
The article is divided on four main parts displayed as 
followed, the first part introduces the scope of the study 
by describing the injection molding process and 
providing an general overview of the application of the 
AHP and the TOPSIS approach in the molding process. 
The second part presents the framework of the proposed 
solution by outlining the various stages of its application, 
the third section, fully dedicated to present the res ults 
obtained after applying the methodology to data collected 
from an ac tual workshop operating in the automotive 
industry, and the last section makes discussion

2. SCOPE OF STUDY AND LITERATURE REVIEW 
 
2. 1. Injection Molding Process          Injection molding 
is an industrial technique, involves injecting plastic 
material into a mold cavity under high pressure, which 
can range from hundreds to thousands of bars  (2). Once 
injected, the plastic cools and solidifies within the mold 
cavity, taking the shape of the mold and producing a 
specific plastic product (10, 11). Figure 1 illustrates the 
five main stages of the standard production cycle. 
To carry out  the manufacturing process, injection 
molding is employed, utilizing a machine that comprises 
several components. These include a hopper for feeding 
the raw plastic material, a heating unit consisting of a 
barrel, screw, and heating resistances to melt the  
material, and an injection unit responsible for injecting 
the molten material into the mold cavity. Additionally, 
the machine features a clamping unit to securely hold the 
mold halves together during the injection and cooling 
phases (12, 13). Furthermore, the machine is equipped 
with controls to regulate temperature, pressure, and other 
parameters, ensuring the production of high-quality parts. 
The clamping Unit (1, 14) is responsible for holding the 
fixed and the moved side of the mold together under 
pressure during the injection and cooling process. It  
consists of a mold, which is mounted on a fixed platen,

and a movable platen which is connected typically to a 
hydraulic system. The clamping unit plays a crucial role 
in maintaining the mold closed during injection, ensuring 
the precision and quality of the molded parts. In contrast, 
the Injection Unit involves a screw mechanism that 
pushes the molten material through a heated barr el and 
into the mold under high pressure (15).  
The principal structure of an injection machine is 
shown in Figure 2.  
 
2. 2 . AHP Approach          The Analytic Hierarchy 
Process (AHP) is a systematic decision-making approach 
pioneered by Thomas Saaty  (16). It is u sed for tackling 
complex problems by decomposing them into a 
hierarchical arrangement of the criteria and also the 
alternatives. AHP involves pairwise comparisons 
between criteria and alternatives based on subjective 
judgments, which are then synthesized to determine their 
relative importance or priority  (17). This process helps 
decision-makers systematically analyze and prioritize 
multiple criteria to arrive at the most suitable decision or 
solution. AHP finds extensive application across diverse 
fields such as engineering, management, and operations 
research, aiding in effective decision-making in scenarios 
characterized by multiple conflicting objectives (18, 19). 
Typically, the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) 
methods can be divided into structured steps, described 
as follows: 
 
2. 2. 1. Problem Structuring           The initial step 
involves establishing the overall goal of the problem, 
listing the criteria, and each sub-criterion associated with 
the main objective. Figure 3 shows the typical 
hierarchical structure of the criteria breakdown. 
 
2. 2. 2. Pairwise Comparisons           The next step 
involves conducting pairwise comparisons between

2. 2. 3. Weighted Score Calculation        In this stage, 
the main objective is to calculate the weighted scores for 
each criteria and alternative by synthesizing the 
judgments made in the pairwise comparisons. This 
involves multiplying the pairwise comparison judgments 
and aggregating them to derive the relative weights (21). 
 
2. 2. 4. Consistency Checking          After completing 
the pairwise comparison, the subsequent step involves 
verifying the accuracy of the comparison by u sing the 
consistency ratio as an indicator (22, 23). 
 
2. 2. 5. Validation           In the validation step, the overall 
score is calculated for each alternative by multiplying the 
priority weights of criteria by the performance scores of 
alternatives for each criterion, and then summing the 
products. Subsequently, in line with the previous step, 
sensitivity analysis is conducted to assess result 
robustness and evaluate how alterations in criteria 
priorities impact alternative rankings

Thorough review of the literature, several gaps and 
opportunities have become apparent, driving the 
development of this paper. The identified literature gap 
in this area can be effectively addressed through the  
 
following three main points: 
 There is a scarcity of research dedicated to the 
utilization of AHP -TOPSIS specifically in the 
context of injection molding processes. While the 
methodology has been extensively explored in other 
domains such as marketing , or in selecting optimal 
tooling for manufacturing, such as EDM electrodes 
for manufacturing as highlighted in source  (43), its 
application within the realm of injection molding 
remains underexplored. This lack of attention is 
significant considering the unique challenges and 
requirements posed by the injection molding 
process, including factors such as material flow, 
cooling rates, mold design, and product quality 
 Many existing studies that combine AHP and 
TOPSIS methodologies do not provide 
comprehensive or detailed calculations of the 
combined methods. This omission undermines the 
transparency and rigor of the decision -making 
process. Without exhaustive calculatio ns, the 
reliability and credibility of the decision -making 
framework are compromised, limiting its practical 
applicability in real-world scenarios 
 Another significant gap in the literature the literature 
is the absence of simultaneous consideration of both 
economic considerations and performance metrics in 
decision-making processes. Often, decision -making 
frameworks fail to incorporate criteria relat ed to the 
economic aspects of manufacturing, including 
factors such as production costs, material costs, labor 
costs, and overhead expenses. Additionally, 
performance metrics of the machinery involved in 
the injection molding process, such as cycle time, 
efficiency, reliability, and maintenance 
requirements, are often overlooked. Ignoring these 
critical aspects can lead to suboptimal decision 
outcomes and missed opportunities for cost savings, 
efficiency improvements, and overall process 
optimization in injection molding operations.
